title: 7 new dementia risk factors revealed — including one millions struggle with
summary: The World Health Organization has added seven new dementia risk factors, including stroke, sleep apnea, HIV and air pollution, to its updated guidelines.
story: Psychiatrist Daniel Amen discusses updated global recommendations for reducing cognitive decline, highlighting hormones, cardiovascular health, restorative rest, sensory loss, social connection and other factors tied to healthy aging.
The World Health Organization (WHO) has released a major update to its guidelines on reducing the risk of cognitive decline and dementia.
The second edition of the original 2019 report was updated to "reflect the latest evidence and advances in dementia risk reduction."
The following seven additional health conditions and exposures were added to the list.
LEARNING ANOTHER LANGUAGE MAY KEEP YOUR BRAIN YOUNGER, STUDY SUGGESTS
Stroke
Traumatic brain injury
Vision impairment
Sleep problems
HIV
Air pollution
Menopausal hormone therapy
The WHO's updated guidelines "reflect the latest evidence and advances in dementia risk reduction." (iStock)
These new risk factors joined the previously existing 12, which are listed below.
Cognitive activity
Social activity
Physical inactivity
Harmful alcohol use
Tobacco use
Unhealthy diet/nutrition
Obesity
Diabetes
Hypertension
Dyslipidemia (abnormal amount of lipids (fats) or lipoproteins in the blood)
Hearing loss
Depression
WARDING OFF ALZHEIMER'S MIGHT MEAN MAKING THESE 11 LIFESTYLE CHANGES, EXPERT SAYS
Dr. Daniel Amen, physician and founder of Amen Clinics in California, has his own formula for reducing Alzheimer’s risk factors, following an acronym called BRIGHT MINDS.

This stands for blood flow, retirement and aging, inflammation, genetics, head trauma, toxins, mental health, immunity and infections, neurohormones, diabesity (co-occurrence of obesity and type 2 diabetes) and sleep. The WHO’s updated guidelines offer similar advice.
Menopausal hormone therapy is primarily used to treat symptoms of menopause. (iStock)
Amen spoke with Fox News Digital about the new additions to the WHO's list of risk factors.
Menopausal hormone therapy (MHT)

The WHO does not recommend menopausal hormone therapy specifically to prevent dementia in postmenopausal women 65 and older. For younger women, it says there is not enough evidence to determine whether MHT affects dementia risk.

Amen agreed that there is not enough evidence to support using MHT specifically to prevent dementia. He said hormonal changes during menopause may affect mood and memory, although the relationship between MHT and dementia risk remains uncertain.
'I'M A NEUROLOGIST — HERE'S WHY DEMENTIA IS RISING AND HOW TO REDUCE YOUR RISK’

"For women, as they go through menopause, lower progesterone makes them anxious, and [with] lower estrogen, they start to have memory problems," he said. "Hormone replacement early on is helpful, and that's what we see on the brain imaging work that we do."
Experts note that while menopause-related hormonal changes can be associated with mood and cognitive symptoms, these effects can vary widely.
Stroke
A stroke occurs when blood flow to part of the brain is blocked or when a blood vessel in or near the brain bursts, according to the American Stroke Association.
Conditions that affect the heart and blood vessels can also affect brain health and are associated with a higher risk of dementia, according to Amen.
Any blood flow blockages can impact brain health and increase the risk of dementia. (iStock)
That can include conditions such as heart disease, heart rhythm problems, stroke and transient ischemic attacks. Erectile dysfunction can also be associated with underlying vascular disease, he said.
"And 40% of 40-year-olds have erectile dysfunction, 70% of 70-year-olds. So, if I'm an older person, I'm thinking if I get my brain right, my love life could be better, too," Amen added.
Traumatic brain injury (TBI)
Amen surmised that the WHO is "late to the party" in emphasizing the importance of head trauma as a dementia risk factor. TBI can range from a mild concussion to a severe brain injury.
COMMON VACCINE LINKED TO 24% LOWER DEMENTIA RISK IN OLDER ADULTS

"One of the big lessons from the brain imaging work we do is that mild traumatic brain injury ruins people's lives," he said. "They end up seeing psychiatrists because they have temper problems or ... depression or anxiety, and it's really from a snowmobiling accident in [their] 30s."
Amen added that failing to protect the brain — which he described as "very soft" and having the consistency of "soft butter" — is "not the smart thing to do."
"Mild traumatic brain injury ruins people's lives," the brain expert said. (iStock)
Vision impairment
A significant portion of the brain is dedicated to vision, according to Amen.
"So, if your vision becomes troubled, your brain's troubled," he said.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

Amen said vision impairment may place additional demands on the brain. While the condition has been linked with cognitive decline, the WHO says there is insufficient evidence to recommend vision treatment specifically for dementia prevention.
Sleep disorders
Sleep appears to support the brain’s waste-clearance processes, Amen noted.
Sleep challenges affect tens of millions of Americans. In 2024, 30.5% of U.S. adults reported getting less than seven hours of shut-eye per day, according to the CDC.
For those with sleep problems such as sleep apnea, it can cause changes in the brain that resemble the hallmarks of Alzheimer’s disease, the expert said.
Research suggests that sleep may help the brain clear beta-amyloid, although the relationship between sleep and dementia remains complex and is still being studied.
HIV
Inflammation and infections can affect brain health. Untreated HIV (human immunodeficiency virus) can affect the central nervous system and is associated with HIV-related cognitive impairment.
"If you love and care for your brain, you're going to love your life a whole bunch more."
Amen said he has scanned "hundreds of people" with HIV, stating that the virus is "clearly a risk factor."

Untreated HIV is known to affect the central nervous system and is associated with HIV-related cognitive impairment. Effective antiretroviral therapy has greatly reduced the incidence of severe HIV-associated dementia.
Air pollution
Exposure to any toxins, from alcohol and marijuana to lead, mercury or air pollution, could be detrimental to brain health, according to Amen.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The WHO recommends reducing exposure to household and outdoor air pollution, particularly fine particulate matter. Research has linked long-term exposure to air pollution with a higher risk of cognitive decline and dementia, although the WHO characterizes the evidence as low to very low certainty.
Exposure to any toxins, from alcohol and marijuana to lead, mercury or air pollution, is detrimental to brain health, the doctor warned. (iStock)
Getting ahead of it
Dementia risk rises sharply with age. A recent U.S. analysis estimated that about one in five people had developed dementia by age 85, with risk increasing further at older ages.
While those with a genetic predisposition to the disease have a higher risk, Amen noted that certain lifestyle factors can increase the risk for anyone.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
"We should be on a dementia prevention program our whole lives," the doctor said. "It’s not something to start when you're 65."
Amen urged everyone to ask themselves the question: "Is what I’m doing good or bad for my brain?"
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
"Social activity is one of the prevention strategies. New learning is a prevention strategy," he added. "So always working on being connected with other people and then just making better decisions."
"If you love and care for your brain, you're going to love your life a whole bunch more."
Angelica Stabile is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: Popular artificial sweetener linked to potentially dangerous heart risk
summary: A new study of over 17,700 participants links higher xylitol blood levels to increased cardiovascular risk, including heart attack and stroke, over future decades.
story: Fox News senior medical analyst Dr. Marc Siegel joins 'Fox & Friends Weekend' to discuss a new study suggesting low sugar intake before age two leads to a reduced risk of developing dementia.
People who consume greater amounts of a popular artificial sweetener could face a greater risk of heart attack and stroke, a new study suggests.

The research, which was presented at the ESC Cardiology Congress in Germany this week, showed that higher levels of xylitol in the blood were associated with an increased risk of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE).

Xylitol is a sugar alcohol that is commonly used as a low-calorie sweetener and sugar substitute, according to the National Institutes of Health. It is often used in higher amounts to sweeten foods, drinks, chewing gum and dental care products.
ZERO-CALORIE SWEETENERS COULD ALTER THE GENES OF LATER GENERATIONS, NEW STUDY WARNS
The researchers followed two large study cohorts of more than 17,700 Canadian and British participants.

Over a six-year follow-up, people in the Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging with the highest xylitol levels had a 57% higher risk of death, myocardial infarction or stroke related to cardiovascular events compared to those with the lowest levels.
People who consume greater amounts of a popular artificial sweetener could face a greater risk of heart attack and stroke, a new study suggests. (iStock)
Over 30 years, participants in the European Prospective Investigation into Cancer (EPIC)-Norfolk group with the highest xylitol levels had an 18% greater risk of MACE.
Both cohorts showed evidence of a dose-dependent association, in which higher blood xylitol concentrations corresponded to higher rates of cardiovascular events.
DIRTY SODA DRINKS ARE EVERYWHERE, BUT DOCTORS WARN OF HEALTH RISKS: 'METABOLIC DISASTER'
These higher risks persisted even after the researchers adjusted for other factors like age, gender, body mass index, hypertension, diabetes and lipid levels.

The study follows previous research that showed xylitol can enhance the ability of platelets to form clots, according to Dr. Marco Witkowski, the study presenter from Charité University Hospital in Berlin, Germany.
Xylitol is a sugar alcohol that is commonly used as a low-calorie sweetener and sugar substitute. (iStock)
"Artificial sweeteners are consumed by people who think they are healthier than sugar, and they are generally regarded as safe by regulatory agencies," the doctor said in a statement.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"Our long-term findings in the general population highlight how little we know about the cardiovascular safety of xylitol and indicate that further studies are warranted, especially as the amount of xylitol in products continues to increase."
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
The study was observational and does not prove that xylitol causes cardiovascular events, as the researchers noted that more studies are needed to confirm the findings.

The report also does not establish whether high levels of xylitol in the blood necessarily reflect dietary consumption, as the sugar alcohol can also be produced naturally in the body as part of glucose metabolism.
People with the highest xylitol levels had a 57% higher risk of death, myocardial infarction or stroke related to cardiovascular events compared to those with the lowest levels. (iStock)

"These disturbing findings with [a] plausible mechanism of xylitol increasing cardiovascular risk should be taken very seriously," Dr. Aseem Malhotra, a cardiologist and public health campaigner based in London, told Fox News Digital.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
"As a practicing cardiologist, I see many patients suffering from anxiety and palpitations that resolve as soon as they stop taking artificial sweeteners."
Malhotra, who was not involved in the study, noted that one of the most important dietary changes to reduce cardiovascular risk is to "unsweeten your sweet tooth."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"That’s why I advise all my patients to avoid all processed sugars and artificial sweeteners for six weeks to break the addiction," he added.
Fox News Digital reached out to several food and beverage trade groups for comment.
Melissa Rudy is senior health editor and a member of the lifestyle team at Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to melissa.rudy@fox.com.

title: Dietitian reveals simple eating strategy for better sleep — and one habit to avoid
summary: Tart cherry juice tops a dietitian's list of sleep-boosting foods, with its natural melatonin content shown to improve both sleep quality and quantity.
story: The New Jersey-based registered dietitian and certified diabetes care specialist says certain foods can make, or break, a good night’s sleep, while a common habit can interfere with rest.
How you eat can influence how you sleep, according to experts.
Erin Palinski-Wade, a New Jersey-based registered dietitian, certified diabetes care specialist and author of "The Sleepdemic Solution," says certain foods can make, or break, a good night’s sleep.
"There are a number of foods that can help support sleep, and sometimes it's even a combination," she told Fox News Digital.
5-STEP SLEEP RESET COULD PROMOTE HEALTHY WEIGHT LOSS, NUTRITIONIST SAYS
Supporting better sleep
Keeping blood sugar steady throughout the day may help prevent afternoon energy crashes and support more restorative sleep at night, Palinski-Wade said.
Waking up in the middle of the night and struggling to fall back asleep may not always be insomnia, she suggested, but could be linked to fluctuations in glucose levels.
Keeping blood sugar steady throughout the day may help prevent afternoon energy crashes and support more restorative sleep at night. (iStock)
Combining lean proteins, slow-digesting carbohydrates and healthy fats in meals and snacks can help stabilize those levels — what Palinski-Wade called the "No. 1 way" to improve overall sleep.
Some small studies suggest tart cherry juice may support sleep, and the expert named tart cherries — or 100% tart cherry juice — as her top choice.
FOOD CRAVINGS AT 3:45 PM AREN'T RANDOM, HERE'S WHAT YOUR BODY MAY BE WARNING YOU ABOUT

"Tart cherries [are] one of the foods that have the highest amount of melatonin naturally, but they also have compounds that help to really extend that melatonin in our bodies and our body's ability to use it," she said.
Still, research linking tart cherry consumption to modest improvements in sleep duration or quality is limited and mixed; a 2025 systematic review reached a similar conclusion.
The expert recommends ingesting 4 to 6 ounces of 100% tart cherry juice or about a quarter cup of dried tart cherries for better sleep. (iStock)
For those who suffer from insomnia, Palinski-Wade recommends ingesting 4 to 6 ounces of 100% tart cherry juice, or about a quarter cup of dried tart cherries.
"It's a really, really great tool to improve your sleep – and it's really tasty, too," she said.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
Foods and drinks that may help reduce inflammation can also support sleep, the dietitian said.
"When we have more antioxidants in the body, more anti-inflammatory compounds, we're really helping our body to achieve that more restful state," Palinski-Wade said.
Foods rich in antioxidants and anti-inflammatory compounds — including nuts and seeds, olive oil and avocados — also provide healthy fats and other nutrients that may support sleep.
Any more than 300 milligrams of caffeine per day becomes a "stressor to our body," the expert warned. (iStock)
Caffeine’s sleep impact
On the other hand, Palinski-Wade warned that caffeine intake can negatively impact sleep quality.

"So many of us have a poor night's sleep and the next day we reach for caffeine to give us a burst of energy," she said. "And there's nothing wrong with a little bit of caffeine, but you have to look at how much you're having and how close to bedtime."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

"And it's a stimulant, so it's harder to fall asleep," Palinski-Wade warned. "If you have foods or beverages with a large amount of caffeine, and you're having them in the afternoon or toward the evening, that is going to make it very hard to get restorative, restful sleep in the evening."
For those who do drink caffeine, it is best to stop about 10 hours before bedtime, the expert advised.
Stimulation and inflammation from caffeine can disrupt sleep if consumed too close to bedtime. (iStock)
The "sweet spot" for daily caffeine intake is 300 milligrams or less, she said. Any more than that becomes a "stressor to our body." A cup of coffee, traditionally 8 ounces, is about 100 milligrams.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

The FDA says up to 400 milligrams daily is not generally associated with negative effects for most adults, although individual tolerance can vary depending on factors such as medications, health conditions and sensitivity to caffeine.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"We start to release stress hormones like cortisol and adrenaline, and that not only makes our body store fat versus burn it, but it also increases inflammation," Palinski-Wade noted.
"So now you have the stimulant, you have this inflammation, and all those things go against quality sleep."
Angelica Stabile is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: Why Dolly Parton’s death can feel like losing someone you knew personally
summary: Fans worldwide describe "post-Parton depression" as Dolly Parton's death triggers intense parasocial grief that psychologists say mirrors real loss.
story: Dolly Parton, the Grammy-winning singer, songwriter and philanthropist whose career spanned over six decades, has died at 80.
The death of Dolly Parton has prompted an outpouring of grief from fans around the world, many of whom have shared that they feel like they’ve lost someone they knew personally.

Grief experts say it’s possible to experience genuine feelings of loss even if there wasn’t a personal relationship — particularly when the public figure has become woven into people’s memories and routines over a long period of time.
Psychologists refer to this type of loss as parasocial grief, according to licensed clinical psychologist Dr. Dara Houp.
DOLLY PARTON’S PRIVATE CANCER BATTLE HIGHLIGHTS WHY SOME PATIENTS DON’T SHARE THEIR DIAGNOSES

"When a celebrity shares their personal life – childhood experiences, hardships and victories – our brains register these bits of information through the same emotional and neural pathways utilized for our real-life friendships and a genuine attachment is developed," Houp, with Pathways Psychological Services in New York City, told Fox News Digital.
When that perceived relationship comes to an end, people may experience the parasocial grief, she said.

\Fans of Dolly Parton visit a mural featuring her likeness in the city's North Side on Aug. 26, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. Fans across the nation are mourning the death of the country music star, actress and philanthropist who died on Tuesday at age 80. (Getty Images)

Desiree Taranto, a licensed mental health counselor and clinical director at Empower Your Mind Therapy in New York City, said the widespread reaction also reflects "collective grief," a shared emotional response when a loss resonates across a community.
"Parton’s music, movies, philanthropy and public persona became part of many people’s family traditions, memories and difficult life moments," she told Fox News Digital.
Fans share their grief

"I honestly didn’t know I could react that way over someone I don’t even personally know," one user wrote in a grief support group on Reddit. "[Dolly] was a ray of sunshine in this dark world nowadays, and I just can’t help but cry and get so emotional about it."
Another user shared that "as each day passes, losing Dolly seems to hurt more instead of less. I have found myself crying and feeling this deep sadness that I just can’t shake."
IN WAKE OF DOLLY PARTON'S DEATH, ONCOLOGIST REVEALS WHY SOME PATIENTS KEEP CANCER DIAGNOSES SECRET
"I never met Dolly, and I know she didn’t know me, but I loved her for most of my life. That love was real, and so this grief feels real too."
Someone else in a different group referred to the feelings of sadness as "post-Parton depression."
Fans honor Dolly Parton with flowers, notes and small gifts at the site of her star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame on Aug. 26, 2026 in Hollywood, California. (Getty Images)
"I don't know why I am taking Dolly Parton's death so hard," one user wrote. "I never met her… She didn't know me. But for some reason, I can't stop crying."
"I think the reason it's hard is because she was a light and just a wonderful human," someone else shared. "She is exactly who Jesus wanted us to be."
Why does it feel personal?
The emotions people experience when grieving a celebrity can feel as real as those felt after losing someone they knew personally, Houp said.

"Perceived relational intimacy, not whether we actually know an individual, is largely what determines the intensity of grief," she said. "The emotional connection your brain developed runs along the same neural pathways as real-life bonds."
"Accept your feelings and know that it is okay to mourn someone you never met."

It’s also possible that the deaths of certain celebrities — particularly those associated with childhood, family traditions or major life moments — are more likely to trigger an intense grief response, the expert noted.

"When a celebrity’s life is connected to a personal milestone — such as a break-up or the birth of a child — their death permanently disrupts a living connection to who, what or where you used to be," Houp said. "Losing a celebrity can feel like losing a piece of your own history."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
A song may be tied to someone who has died, a family memory or a difficult period when Parton’s work brought comfort, Taranto noted, making the loss feel connected to a person’s own life story.
Over decades in the public eye, Parton gave fans a window into her life, allowing them to form a sense of who she was, Houp said.
Fans pay tribute to Dolly Parton at her home in Brentwood on Aug. 25, 2026 in Brentwood, Tennessee. (Getty Images)
"For many who followed Dolly’s life, she represented resilience and ambition, authenticity and bold self-expression, and a rare, unconditional kindness," she said.
"We identified with the goodness we saw in Dolly and felt encouraged by her ability to overcome hardship – thereby furthering our sense of connection to her."
Tips to navigate grief
Taranto offered advice for those feeling the grief following Parton’s death.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

"Accept your feelings and know that it is okay to mourn someone you never met," she said. "Do not judge yourself or feel embarrassed because that person’s work, values or advocacy touched your life personally."
It can also help to reach out to others who are also grieving the loss.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
"Be there for each other and allow others to be there for you," Taranto advised. "Tell stories, listen to her music, watch her movies or journal about what she meant to you."
"Remember the positive impact she made in the world and the ways she used her platform for good. Shared grief can help us process a loss because it reminds us that we are not alone in it."
Melissa Rudy is senior health editor and a member of the lifestyle team at Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to melissa.rudy@fox.com.

title: Arizona voter-law fight reaches SCOTUS as election groups warn ‘absurd’ consequence could ensue
summary: Election experts warn the Supreme Court that the Ninth Circuit's ruling could make it impossible to ever remove noncitizens from state voter rolls.
story: Federal prosecutors charge a Honduran national with voter fraud in California after he allegedly registered to vote under an alias and cast ballots in multiple elections. Fox News' Matt Finn reports on the federal indictment details, revealing the suspect received a voter registration card using a gym membership. The case highlights ongoing debates surrounding voter identification laws.

Election experts are warning the Supreme Court that affirming a lower court's ruling could mean that noncitizens, minors, or factitious people listed on state voter rolls could be impossible to remove.

The Supreme Court is set to hear oral arguments in RNC v. Mi Familia Vote this December and will determine whether a pair of Arizona's state laws which remove the registrations of noncitizen voters from voter rolls within 90 days of the election and require voters to show proof of U.S. citizenship when registering to vote are in violation of the National Voter Registration Act.

"Citizenship is a qualification for voting. If states are going to enforce that requirement, they have to be able to verify it," Justin Riemer, president & CEO of Restoring Integrity and Trust in Elections said in a statement to Fox News Digital. "And when officials find noncitizens on the voter rolls, they should be able to act before an election, not after. We are confident the Supreme Court will agree and reverse the Ninth Circuit's misguided ruling."

In an amicus brief filed on Thursday, attorneys from Center for Election Confidence, Inc., Restoring Integrity and Trust in Elections, Inc., and Honest Elections Project, argued that the Ninth Circuit Court's ruling that the Arizona laws are an act of "voter suppression" is "absurd" and raises serious threats to state rights.

FILE - Voters arrive to the polling location at the Burton Barr Central Library on November 05, 2024 in Phoenix, Arizona. RNC v. Mi Familia Vote will determine whether a pair of Arizona's state laws which remove the registrations of noncitizen voters from voter rolls within 90 days of the election and require voters to show proof of U.S. citizenship when registering to vote are in violation of the National Voter Registration Act. (Photo by Christian Petersen/Getty Images)
CLINTON-APPOINTED JUDGE TRIGGERS APPEAL AFTER BLOCKING KEY VOTER CITIZENSHIP LAW

The brief argued that Congress may regulate the mechanics of federal elections, but states have the constitutional authority to set and enforce voter qualifications — a power they argued becomes meaningless if states cannot obtain documentation needed to verify citizenship or remove people who were never eligible to register.

"Since the power to establish voting requirements is of little value without the power to enforce those requirements, it would raise serious constitutional doubts if a federal statute precluded a State from obtaining the information necessary to enforce its voter qualifications," the brief stated.

The amicus brief pushed back on the Ninth Circuit’s conclusion that Arizona cannot conduct a systematic program to remove noncitizens from voter rolls during the NVRA’s 90-day pre-election period. The federal law generally requires states to complete systematic voter-removal programs at least 90 days before a federal election, while allowing removals during that window for a voter’s request, death, criminal conviction or mental incapacity.
DEMOCRAT NEW JERSEY GOVERNOR SAYS THOUSANDS OF NONCITIZENS DISCOVERED ON VOTER ROLLS, PURGED

FILE - A volunteer picks up "Require Voter ID" sign at the press conference at the Riverside County Registrar of Voters on Monday, March 2, 2026, as GOP lawmakers gather in support of placing a voter ID measure on the November ballot. (Anjali Sharif-Paul/MediaNews Group/The Sun via Getty Images)

The groups argued that non-citizenship is not among those listed grounds because it concerns someone who was never eligible to register in the first place. They said the restriction is meant to protect eligible voters from erroneous last-minute removals — not to shield people who were never eligible to register.

"If the Ninth Circuit is right that the 90-day limitation on programs prohibits removal on these bases — because the statute has listed exceptions — States could never remove improperly registered individuals who fall within these categories, no matter when the removal happens or whether it is after a systematic inquiry," the brief said.
"Not just that, but these States could never remove these noncitizens who were never eligible to vote," the brief continued.

The brief pointed to reported registration errors in New Jersey, Illinois and Oregon as examples of why states need a mechanism to correct allegedly improper registrations. It argues that an unlawful ballot cannot be undone once cast and counted.
DHS APPROVES PLAN TO VERIFY VOTER CITIZENSHIP, MONITOR MAIL BALLOTS AS TRUMP PUSH INTENSIFIES

"American elections are for American citizens only. Period," Lisa Dixon, executive director of the Center for Election Confidence, said in a statement. "We should all support Arizona ensuring non-citizens can’t register to vote and removing any non-citizens who end up on the voter lists."

The amici also argued that the Ninth Circuit misread NVRA provisions governing what information is "necessary" for state election officials to assess a voter’s eligibility, and whether a state registration form is "equivalent" to the federal form.

FILE - Security guards stand in front of the Ninth U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals in San Francisco, Calif., on June 12, 2017. The brief argued that the Ninth Circuit wrongly concluded a voter’s citizenship attestation on a registration form is sufficient proof of eligibility. (Getty Images)

The brief argued that the Ninth Circuit wrongly concluded a voter’s citizenship attestation on a registration form is sufficient proof of eligibility and improperly interpreted an "equivalent" state form to mean one that is virtually identical to the federal form.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"Once again, far-left activists are using the courts to twist federal law into a straitjacket that prevents states from securing their elections," Jason Snead, executive director of Honest Elections Project, said in a statement to Fox News. "The Honest Elections Project urges the Supreme Court to side with Arizona and preserve the tools states need to ensure that elections are decided only by American citizens."
Elaine Mallon is a writer for Fox News Digital and Fox Business covering national politics.

title: Well-connected Dem operative learns fate after FBI busts him in child sex abuse sting
summary: A former Virginia Democratic Party finance chair and 2024 DNC delegate was handed a decade behind bars for child sexual abuse material and other child sex abuse allegations.
story: Democratic consultant Julian Epstein and former RNC general counsel Alex Vogel join 'Fox News Live' to analyze Democratic candidates rejecting campaign appearances from Joe Biden and Kamala Harris after new polling data was revealed.

A well-connected political consultant in Virginia with ties to the state's Democratic Party was sentenced to 10 years in federal prison after getting caught with child sexual abuse material and attempting to sexually abuse an undercover agent's purported 9-year-old son in an undercover FBI child sex abuse sting.

Randon Sprinkle, 31, of Richmond, was handed the decade-long sentence on Thursday by U.S. District Judge Roderick C. Young following a federal investigation by the FBI’s Child Exploitation and Human Trafficking Task Force, according to a Justice Department press release. According to the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Eastern District of Virginia, Sprinkle was ensnared in a May 2025 undercover operation after making contact on a dating app called Jack'd with an agent posing as the father of a 9-year-old boy.

Authorities said Sprinkle sent the undercover agent a video showing two adults sexually abusing a minor, voiced a desire to travel to Washington, D.C., to abuse the fictitious child, and was later found in possession of dozens of files depicting the sexual abuse of toddlers and infants when agents searched his home.
FBI RAIDS SPANBERGER ALLY OFFICE AS FEDERAL CORRUPTION PROBE TARGETS CANNABIS BUSINESS
Virginia Democratic operative Randon Sprinkle received a 10-year federal prison sentence for child sexual abuse charges. (Getty Images)

Beyond serving as the finance chairman for the Democratic Party of Virginia and the treasurer for the Metro Richmond Area Young Democrats, Sprinkle served as an elected delegate to the 2024 Democratic National Convention, according to public party rosters and local reporting. He also worked as a paid political director for Rep. Jennifer McClellan’s 2021 gubernatorial bid and previously served as her legislative aide when she was a state senator.
Meanwhile, Sprinkle has also worked for other Virginia Democratic Party campaigns, according to consulting payments, including state Sen. Jennifer Boysko.
The Virginia General Assembly will convene for 2024 with a slim Democratic majority here at the Virginia Capitol in Richmond, Va. (AP Photo/Steve Helber, File)

State campaign finance records compiled by the Virginia Public Access Project (VPAP) also show Sprinkle, who worked as an associate for the Richmond-based Reflex Strategy Group and another consulting group called Alexander Strategies LLC, donated thousands of dollars to the recent statewide campaigns of Rep. Abigail Spanberger and Lt. Gov. Ghazala Hashmi.

Alleged photos preserved online following his arrest show Sprinkle regularly operating alongside national-level Democratic Party politicians as well, including former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, whose name has been floated for a presidential run in 2028, Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer, and Spanberger, among others.
Spanberger's transition team previously released a statement after his arrest, thanking the FBI "for their investigative work and for bringing this predator to justice."

"As a former federal law enforcement officer who arrested child predators, she believes that this individual should be swiftly prosecuted and put behind bars for his sickening crimes against children," the statement said. "Upon learning about these appalling reports, the Spanberger campaign immediately donated the full amount of this individual’s prior donations, $1000, to the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children to support its critical mission of protecting America’s kids."
ILLEGAL ALIEN'S ‘INEXCUSABLE’ CRIME SPARKS INTERSTATE CLASH BETWEEN GOP SEN, DEM GOV: ‘YOU SHOULD BE ASHAMED’

When reached for comment, the Metro Richmond Area Young Democrats referred Fox News Digital to a statement issued by the organization’s executive board following Sprinkle's initial indictment in December 2025, confirming they took "immediate action to terminate all ties."

"The alleged conduct outlined in the indictment is reprehensible, unforgivable, and fundamentally misaligned with the values of our organization," the board said in the statement. "It violates the most basic standards of humanity and decency."
Randon Sprinkle was arrested after being busted in an undercover FBI child sex abuse sting. (iStock)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Fox News Digital also reached out to the Democratic Party of Virginia and the public defender representing him but did not hear back in time for publication. .
Alec Schemmel is a Politics Reporter for Fox News Digital who is originally from Charlotte, North Carolina but now resides in the Washington D.C.-Baltimore Metro Area.

title: Ex-Fetterman staffers promise more damaging details after blistering report: ‘Tip of the iceberg’
summary: Former staffers for John Fetterman launched an X account promising damaging revelations well beyond the Wall Street Journal report.
story: Sen. John Fetterman, D-Pa., issued a fiery rebuttal to former Maine Democratic Senate candidate Graham Platner after he dropped out of the race following sexual assault allegations on ‘Jesse Watters Primetime.’
In just over a week, former staffers for John Fetterman, D-Pa., are planning to go public with inside details after expressing what they called disgust at his work as a legislator.

"We’re a group of former campaign & Senate staffers for John Fetterman who are disgusted with what he's become. If you were troubled by yesterday's Wall Street Journal story... trust us, that's just the tip of the iceberg," the group wrote in a post to X.
"It’s even worse than you thought."

The new social media account, which is calling itself "Former Fetterman Staffers" (FFS) alleges it will reveal additional unflattering details of the embattled senator’s office as he also faces blowback over Wall Street Journal reporting chronicling his reluctance to engage in the basic duties of his office.
FETTERMAN FACES DEM REVOLT AS BOMBSHELL REPORT FUELS PUSH TO OUST HIM: 'DISGRACE'

Sen. John Fetterman, a Democrat from Pennsylvania, speaks to members of the media after a vote at the US Capitol in Washington, DC, US, on Tuesday, July 22, 2025. With their summer recess beckoning, lawmakers will try to pack as much must-do work as possible into the week ahead. Photographer (Eric Lee/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
The FFS acronym notoriously also stands for "for f---s sake."

Fetterman routinely blew off constituent meetings, neglected legislative review and declined to make in-state public appearances, according to a Wall Street Journal report published on Thursday, drawing immediate backlash online.

"There is a lot I could say about this report of John Fetterman’s pathetic behavior as a senator," Rep. Chris Deluzio, D-Pa., said on X. "But between the laziness, disrespect, and willingness to carry water for a foreign government, it shows us something we already know: this man has no sense of duty."
"John Fetterman is a disgrace," Rep. Brendan Boyle, D-Pa., said in a post of his own. "Our state deserves better than a lazy trust fund baby who is too lazy to do the job."
Pennsylvania state Rep. Malcolm Kenyatta, who is the vice chair of the Democratic National Committee, also condemned Fetterman’s behavior.
"This report is horrifying, but not new to many of us in PA. John barely showed up as [Lieutenant Governor] and is constantly MIA as our senator," Kenyatta wrote.
"When he’s not on FOX cheerleading Trump & endless wars, he is attacking the very neighbors who gave him a chance. 2028 can’t come soon enough," he continued.
DNC VICE CHAIR ATTACKS DEMOCRATIC SEN. JOHN FETTERMAN: 'YOU’RE A MESS'

Senator John Fetterman (D-PA) speaks to reporters following a briefing by Trump administration officials to members of the Senate on U.S. strikes on Iran, at the U.S. Capitol in Washington, DC on March 3, 2026 (Nathan Posner/Anadolu via Getty Images)
Conor Lamb, a former Pennsylvania congressman who ran against Fetterman in the 2022 primary for the party’s nomination, called on Fetterman to resign.

"John, if there is a decent bone left in your body, just quit. It’s an insult to decent people in our state for you to treat them and the office this way," Lamb wrote, referring to an instance where Fetterman blew off a meeting with paralyzed military veterans.
As reactions continue to pour in, Former Fetterman Staffers, the new group on X, told viewers that they would set a deadline for some of its upcoming revelations.
"Set your calendar for September 14th -- the day the Senate is back in session -- for our first drop. (Let's be honest, maybe the 15th: he'll skip Monday's votes)," the group said.
Despite raising questions and rage towards Fetterman, some observers condemned the staffers for what they called a lack of loyalty.

"So disloyal. He gave you jobs and opportunities and advanced your careers, and you publicly turn on him and set up an X account to attack him?" Marc Thiessen, a political pundit and former White House speechwriter for the Bush Administration, wrote on X.
"Honorable thing, if you disagree, is to resign quietly and work for someone else you prefer. You are pathetic," he continued.
Mark Morgan, political director for the Republican Governors Association, echoed Thiessen's thinking, blasting the group for its anonymity.

"Staff rule #1: it's not about you Staff rule #2: Your boss had the courage to put their name on a ballot. If you've chosen to become a click-seeking bottom feeder, at least have the courage to put your own name on it," Morgan said.
EMBATTLED REP TONY GONZALES ANNOUNCES PLANS TO RESIGN AMID SEXUAL MISCONDUCT ALLEGATIONS
U.S. Sen. John Fetterman, D-Pa., speaks to reporters outside the Senate Chamber during votes on Nov. 10, 2025 on Capitol Hill in Washington, D.C. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)
"I’m disgusted by anonymous leakers, actually," Harmeet Dhillon, Trump's assistant attorney general for the Civil Rights Division at the U.S. Department of Justice, also chimed in.

Fetterman’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Fox News Digital.
Leo Briceno is a politics reporter for the congressional team at Fox News Digital. He was previously a reporter with World Magazine.

title: NJ mayor demands sanctuary policy rollback after baby killed in crash allegedly involving illegal immigrant
summary: Jackson Township's mayor says New Jersey's Immigrant Trust Directive must be rolled back after an unlicensed illegal immigrant allegedly killed a baby.
story: Jackson Township Mayor Jennifer Kuhn criticized the sanctuary policies of New Jersey after authorities say an illegal immigrant driving in her town hit a family with her car, killing a 9-month-old boy.

The mayor of the New Jersey township where a baby boy was killed last week after an illegal immigrant allegedly struck the child's family with her car in a grocery store parking lot told Fox News Digital that the state's sanctuary policies should be rolled back to help prevent similar tragedies.

"If our police pull somebody over and they're undocumented... they can't call the federal agencies, they can't call ICE. That needs to change," Jennifer Kuhn, the mayor of Jackson Township, said in an interview on Thursday. "Condolences at this point are not enough. At this point, leadership needs to step in. And we have to do something."

Authorities say Maria Cobon-Guzman, a Guatemalan national who did not have a driver's license, hit a mother pushing a stroller carrying her 9-month-old son and 5-year-old daughter in the parking lot of a kosher grocery store in Jackson on Aug. 28. The infant died, while the mother and 5-year-old were critically injured.
Kuhn argued the crash underscores the need to scrap New Jersey policies that, in most cases, limit cooperation between local, county and state law enforcement and federal immigration authorities.
ILLEGAL ALIEN'S ‘INEXCUSABLE’ CRIME SPARKS INTERSTATE CLASH BETWEEN GOP SEN, DEM GOV: ‘YOU SHOULD BE ASHAMED’

Jennifer Kuhn, the mayor of Jackson Township, New Jersey. She has condemned the sanctuary city policies of former Gov. Phil Murphy and current Gov. Mikie Sherrill, both Democrats. (Courtesy of Mayor Jennifer Kuhn)
"These issues shouldn't happen whether you're illegal or legal. But the problem is that we can't hold them accountable if they're not documented and they're illegal aliens," she added.

Cobon-Guzman, 20, was charged with manslaughter. Prosecutors also charged Ariadna Lazaro-Flores, alleging she allowed Cobon-Guzman to drive her vehicle despite knowing she did not have a driver's license.
Lazaro-Flores, an illegal immigrant from Mexico, was charged with endangering the welfare of an incompetent person, according to an inmate report.

The booking photos of Maria Cobon-Guzman, left, and Ariadana Lazaro-Flores, right. Cobon-Guzman was charged with manslaughter after authorities say she ran her car into a family of three in a grocery store parking lot in Jackson, New Jersey, on Aug. 28. Lazaro-Flores was charged as well, for allegedly letting Cobon-Guzman drive the car knowing she did not have a valid license. (Ocean County Sheriff's Office)

Both women illegally entered the U.S. during the Biden administration, with Lazaro-Flores doing so five times in October 2023 and being removed each time, the Department of Homeland Security previously told Fox News Digital.
Cobon-Guzman entered once in October 2023 but was released unvetted into the nation’s interior, DHS added. On July 31, an immigration judge issued an order of removal against her.
DEADLY ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT TRUCK CRASH EXPOSED FAILURES ON THE ROAD AND AT THE BORDER: KEY SENATOR
At the center of Kuhn's criticism is New Jersey's Immigrant Trust Directive, a policy implemented under former Gov. Phil Murphy in 2018.

Among other provisions, the directive generally prohibits police from asking about a person's immigration status, notifying U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) when someone is being released from custody, or sharing certain non-public personal information for civil immigration enforcement purposes.

Current New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill signed legislation codifying the directive into state law in March. She also signed an executive order in February that prohibits ICE agents from using nonpublic areas of state property to stage or conduct operations unless they have a judicial warrant.

New Jersey Gov.-elect Mikie Sherrill and Gov. Phil Murphy greet the audience before a conversation between Stephen Colbert and Conan O'Brien to benefit Montclair Film at New Jersey Performing Arts Center in Newark, N.J., on Dec. 7, 2025. (Getty Images)
NJ TAXPAYERS ON THE HOOK FOR $12M MORE AS DEM GOVERNOR PROTECTS ILLEGAL ALIENS BATTLING DEPORTATION
Kuhn is calling for the Jackson Township Council to pass a resolution demanding an end to such policies at the state level.
"I know that there's other towns around in Ocean County and in other counties that are also doing the same. Something needs to change," Kuhn said.

Supporters of the policies say they help build trust between immigrant communities and local law enforcement by encouraging victims and witnesses to report crimes without fear that routine interactions with police will lead to scrutiny over their immigration status.
Dan Prochilo, a spokesperson for the New Jersey Attorney General's Office, defended the Immigrant Trust Directive and other sanctuary-style reforms signed by Sherrill.
New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill speaks in the Assembly Chamber of the New Jersey State House in Trenton, New Jersey, on March 10, 2026. (Heather Khalifa/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

County jails and state prisons can notify ICE when someone is being released if they are charged with or have been convicted of certain violent or serious crimes, Prochilo said in a statement to Fox News Digital.
Some of those crimes include assault, stalking, criminal sexual contact, arson and burglary, according to the Immigrant Trust Directive.
New Jersey jails can also notify ICE if a suspect has been convicted of a felony within the past five years or is under a final deportation order from a federal immigration judge, Prochilo said.
