title: What Meta's new teen restrictions mean for young people
summary: Meta's new teen accounts settlement sets a default two-hour daily limit on Instagram and Facebook, plus night mode and school mode restrictions.
story: Tech policy expert Clare Morell joins 'Fox & Friends' to analyze the impact of Meta's youth addiction settlement, which mandates a two-hour daily limit for Facebook and Instagram users under 18. The historic agreement blocks apps from midnight to 6 a.m. and silences school-hour notifications.
If you have ever asked a teenager to put down a phone and heard, "Just one more minute," you already know how hard screen limits can be to enforce.
Now Meta has agreed to a sweeping child-safety settlement that could reshape how teens use Facebook and Instagram across much of the United States.

A judge approved the agreement on Aug. 27. Under the deal, Meta will put a default two-hour daily cap on teen use of Facebook and Instagram combined. It will also restrict most app access overnight. Meanwhile, parents will get stronger control over settings teens may want to change.
The agreement goes well beyond a screen time reminder. Here's what will change, how the limits work, what Meta told CyberGuy and what parents can do now.
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the Protect Your Money replay

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, Protect Your Money From Today’s Biggest Threats , has ended, but you can still watch the full replay and download our financial protection checklist. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five simple ways to help defend yourself against AI scams, fraud, identity theft and financial hacks. You’ll learn how to set up bank alerts, strengthen your account logins, protect your phone number, freeze your credit and help secure your retirement savings against unauthorized transfers. No technical experience is needed.
Get the free replay and checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com
TOO MUCH SCREEN TIME MAY TRIGGER LASTING BRAIN DELAYS, TOP HEALTH OFFICIAL WARNS
Meta says teen accounts will continue using age-appropriate content settings while the company strengthens protections for younger users. (Meta)
How Meta's new restrictions could change a teen's day

With the judge's approval, the agreement is now in effect, but the new protections will roll out over the coming months. Most of the major requirements have a six-month compliance deadline, while some features are due sooner. Here's how the biggest changes break down for teens and parents.

Meta will apply a default two-hour daily limit across Facebook and Instagram combined. Time spent scrolling on either app counts toward the total. In addition, Meta says it will count usage across multiple accounts when it detects that one teen operates more than one account.

Direct messaging, time spent in settings and qualifying long-form audio or video are excluded from the two-hour limit. Under the agreement, qualifying long-form content generally means audio or video that lasts at least 22 minutes and has not been artificially extended.
A teen can only turn off the two-hour limit with a parent's permission. That creates a much firmer stopping point than another reminder that can be dismissed.
Meta already offers parental time-management tools on Instagram, while the proposed settlement would add a default two-hour daily limit across Facebook and Instagram. (Meta)
Night Mode will block most Facebook and Instagram activity from midnight to 6 a.m. During that window, teens will no longer be able to view or post to areas such as Feed, Stories, Explore or Reels.

Direct messaging will remain available. That exception lets teens continue communicating with friends and family. For families dealing with late-night scrolling, this could create a clearer boundary without requiring someone to change the setting every evening.
Meta will also disable push notifications by default from 10 p.m. to 7 a.m., except for urgent account security or platform integrity alerts. Parents using supervision can change that setting.
School Mode focuses on daytime distractions. From 8 a.m. to 3 p.m. Monday through Friday between Aug. 15 and June 15, Meta will mute most push notifications by default.

However, teens will still be able to receive direct messages. Meta will also allow account security and safety alerts during those hours. The idea is simple. A school day should come with fewer reasons to keep checking Instagram or Facebook.

Meta will also add more frequent reminders. Teens will receive a prompt after every 15 minutes of continuous screen time on Facebook or Instagram. In addition, Meta will send prompts when total daily use reaches 60 minutes and again at 90 minutes.
The settlement requires these prompts and pauses to be implemented within four months of the agreement's effective date.
Those alerts arrive before a teen reaches the two-hour limit. As a result, the hard cap becomes the final boundary rather than the first warning.

The agreement also changes parts of the viewing experience. Teens will be able to choose a non-personalized feed as their default. That feed will avoid Meta's recommendation systems when deciding what to show next.

Parents using supervision will be able to require that setting. Meta will also periodically remind teens that the option exists. Meanwhile, teens will be able to turn off autoplay. Parents will be able to require that setting too. With autoplay disabled, another piece of content will no longer begin automatically. The teen will need to tap or swipe to continue.
NEW MEXICO SEEKS MASSIVE PENALTY FROM META AFTER JURY FOUND TECH GIANT LIABLE FOR ENDANGERING CHILDREN
Instagram gives teens ways to shape what they see, while the new agreement adds more controls around how young users experience Meta’s apps. (Meta)
Meta will hide like and reaction totals by default for teen accounts. That applies to a teen's own posts as well as content posted by other people.

The company is also expanding its restrictions on appearance filters. Meta already blocks teens from using cosmetic surgery filters. Under the agreement, teens will also lose access to what Meta calls extreme makeup filters. These changes target parts of the social media experience that can keep attention focused on appearance and social feedback.
Age verification sits at the center of these protections. A teen limit only works if the platform correctly identifies the person behind the account.

Meta says it will invest in stronger technology to find accounts that may belong to children under 13. The company also plans to improve systems that identify users ages 13 to 17 who enter an adult birthday. Once Meta identifies those accounts, it can place them into experiences designed for teens.
Still, age detection remains one of the biggest tests ahead. A system that regularly mistakes teens for adults could weaken many of the protections in the agreement.

Meta also plans to expand its parental supervision tools. For example, parents will receive a notification when a teen links a secondary account. The company also plans alerts involving interactions with accounts it considers potentially suspicious.

In addition, parents will get periodic updates about their teen's usage and attempts to change protective settings. Those alerts could make it easier to catch changes without constantly checking a teen's account.
Meta’s Teen Accounts include built-in privacy and safety settings, with parents able to help manage certain protections for users under 18. (Meta)
Meta's Teen Accounts already laid the groundwork

Meta began rolling out Teen Accounts in 2024. Those accounts brought automatic protections to younger Instagram users and added more control for parents. Meta later expanded its teen safety approach across more of its services.
CyberGuy previously covered Meta's expansion of Teen Accounts to Facebook and Messenger. Earlier tools leaned more heavily on reminders and configurable controls.

By comparison, the settlement creates stronger defaults. A teen who reaches the two-hour combined limit will need a parent's permission to turn it off. For a household where "five more minutes" somehow turns into another hour, that could feel very different.
Why TikTok and YouTube are tied to Meta's payout
Meta describes the financial package as approximately $18 billion. Participating states would receive about 70% of the allocated payment, or roughly $12.7 billion, over 10 years.

The remaining 30%, about $5.3 billion, depends on TikTok and YouTube meeting two conditions. First, both companies would need to implement a one-hour Daily Limit, Night Mode and age-assurance measures. Second, each would need to make a matching financial payment.

Half of Meta's remaining funds would be tied to YouTube's payment. The other half would depend on TikTok. Meta argues that restricting teens on one platform has limited impact if they can immediately move to another app. That helps explain why two of its biggest rivals play such a prominent role in the agreement.

The executed agreement also includes Snap in the broader industry-adoption framework. However, Meta's public explanation ties the matching financial-payment requirement specifically to TikTok and YouTube.
Meta is calling on TikTok and YouTube to adopt similar teen protections, including daily time limits, overnight restrictions and stronger age checks. (Meta)
Meta calls for an industry-wide approach

Meta responded to CyberGuy with additional information about the agreement, including an open letter calling on TikTok and YouTube to adopt the same framework. According to Meta, teens regularly move among many apps, so similar protections need to extend across the industry.

Meta Chief Legal Officer C.J. Mahoney made the same case in an on-camera statement provided to CyberGuy. He said, " Because teens move fluidly across dozens of apps, we need an industry-wide solution."

Mahoney also called on TikTok and YouTube to implement the framework right away. From a parent's point of view, Meta's argument is easy to understand. If Instagram closes after two hours while another social platform stays available, some teens may simply move their scrolling somewhere else.
That position also helps explain why TikTok and YouTube play such a prominent role in the settlement's financial structure.
Limits get tougher if other platforms join

Participation from Snap, TikTok and YouTube could trigger stricter Meta limits under the agreement's broader industry-adoption framework. The agreement requires most of its provisions to remain in place for 10 years. However, Meta's Time Limit and Night Mode commitments initially run for five years.
If industry peers join the agreement, those commitments extend to 10 years. The defaults would get tougher too.
Meta says the Daily Limit would drop to one hour per app. Night Mode would expand from midnight through 6 a.m. to 10 p.m. through 7 a.m.
As a result, participation from Meta's rivals could change both the length and strength of the restrictions.
Meta wants app stores involved in age checks

Meta says social media platforms should not shoulder the entire age-verification process on their own. The company argues that app stores should provide developers with verified age information. According to Meta, that could help apps apply age-appropriate protections more consistently.

Meta also supports legislation that would require app stores to verify a user's age and obtain parental approval before a teen downloads an app. That debate could become increasingly important as more platforms introduce age-based restrictions.
Independent auditors will check Meta's compliance
The agreement also creates outside oversight. An independent auditor will test Meta's compliance and report to participating states. Those reviews will happen annually for five years.

Meta says the agreement will also establish an independent social media research foundation. The company says it will provide consented user data to the foundation for research into teen well-being. That outside review could help show whether the protections work once they reach millions of accounts.
Tips to help protect your teen right now

A judge approved the settlement on Aug. 27. While the new requirements will roll out over the coming months, families can review their teen's social media settings today. Here are several places to start.

Meta's supervision tools give parents access to additional controls and account information. Once supervision is connected, parents can review available safety settings and manage certain protections. CyberGuy has steps showing you how to activate Instagram's parental supervision tools and link your teen's account. Before changing everything, talk with your teen about the settings you plan to use. Explain what you want to protect and why.

Open the phone's screen-time dashboard and look at the numbers together. You may discover that Instagram or Facebook takes up less time than expected. Another app could be responsible for a much larger share of the day. Then, use those numbers to set limits that reflect how the phone is actually being used. CyberGuy has a deeper guide to phone safety tools for parents, including screen-time controls.

Look at who can follow, message or tag your teen. Meta says it will continue using private defaults for teen Instagram accounts. Facebook will also keep restrictive default settings for teens. Meanwhile, the company plans to make it harder for potentially suspicious adults to find or interact with younger users. Also review followers your teen no longer recognizes.

Meta says teens will remain in age-appropriate content settings by default. The company also plans to continue restricting interactions with accounts it considers inappropriate for younger users. Parents using supervision should check those controls periodically.

Facebook and Instagram make up only part of a teen's digital day. Apple Screen Time and Google Family Link can add device-level limits. Those controls become especially useful when a teen moves from one social app to another. As a result, parents can create boundaries that extend beyond Meta's platforms.

Meta's Night Mode will add an overnight barrier inside Facebook and Instagram. Families can add another layer by charging phones outside bedrooms or keeping them in a shared space overnight. A simple routine can also reduce the nightly debate over when the phone goes away.
What these restrictions could mean for teens and parents
The two-hour cap will probably grab the most attention because it creates a clear stopping point. However, the bigger change may be how many of these protections will start turned on by default.
For teens, that could mean more interruptions during long scrolling sessions, fewer overnight opportunities to browse feeds and less pressure from notifications during school hours.
Parents will also gain more visibility when a teen tries to change certain settings. Meanwhile, Meta will face independent compliance reviews during part of the agreement period.

Age detection remains a key challenge. If a 15-year-old can easily convince the system that an account belongs to an adult, many of these protections become much easier to avoid. For that reason, the rollout will tell us far more than the announcement alone.
Kurt's key takeaways

I have watched social media companies add parental controls for years. One recurring problem keeps coming up: Parents have to find the controls before those tools can help. This agreement puts more protections on by default. A two-hour limit that requires parental permission to disable feels very different from another screen-time reminder. The overnight block could also give families some backup when late-night scrolling becomes a constant battle. I understand Meta's argument about TikTok and YouTube too. If one app closes the door while other major platforms remain available, a teen may simply move on to the next feed. Still, the real test comes as these protections roll out over the coming months. I want to see how accurately Meta identifies teen accounts and how difficult these limits are to bypass. Parents should view these tools as backup, not autopilot. Settings can create useful boundaries, but conversations at home still have to carry much of the load.

title: Healthcare data breach exposes 3.75M patient records
summary: The CareCloud data breach exposed Social Security numbers, banking information and medical records belonging to more than 3.75 million people.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

You can be careful with your passwords and still get caught in a breach at a company you may have never heard of. That is one of the frustrating parts of the CareCloud data breach. More than 3.75 million people had personal information and medical records stolen after hackers gained access to a CareCloud cloud environment earlier this year.

CareCloud provides electronic medical record technology and other services to tens of thousands of healthcare providers across the U.S. So, even if you never created a CareCloud account, a doctor's office or another healthcare provider could have used its technology to handle your information. Now, we are getting a much clearer picture of just how much information hackers took.
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the Protect Your Money replay

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, Protect Your Money From Today’s Biggest Threats , has ended, but you can still watch the full replay and download our financial protection checklist. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five simple ways to help defend yourself against AI scams, fraud, identity theft and financial hacks. You’ll learn how to set up bank alerts, strengthen your account logins, protect your phone number, freeze your credit and help secure your retirement savings against unauthorized transfers. No technical experience is needed.
Get the free replay and checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com
INSURANCE BREACH EXPOSES 7M DRIVER'S LICENSES
Healthcare providers rely on digital systems to store and manage sensitive patient information, making security a critical part of protecting medical records. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
CareCloud data breach affects more than 3.75 million people

The cyberattack dates back to March 2026. According to a breach notice filed with the California Attorney General, CareCloud experienced a network disruption on March 16. The company brought in outside cybersecurity experts to investigate. CareCloud later determined that an unauthorized third party had access to one of its Amazon Web Services environments between March 10 and March 16, 2026.

The company said the attacker claimed to have taken data from databases inside that environment. CareCloud also said it found no evidence of continued unauthorized activity after March 16. Early disclosures showed hundreds of thousands of people were affected. However, that figure later climbed dramatically. CareCloud has now reported that more than 3.75 million people were affected, according to federal health regulators. The disclosure places the incident among the largest healthcare data breaches reported so far in 2026.
What hackers stole in the CareCloud data breach

Here is where this breach becomes especially concerning. The stolen information goes well beyond an email address or phone number. What was exposed varies from person to person, but the data may include:
Names and postal addressesSocial Security numbersMedical and health informationDriver's license numbers, passport information and other government-issued IDsBanking and other financial information
Names and postal addresses
Social Security numbers
Medical and health information
Driver's license numbers, passport information and other government-issued IDs
Banking and other financial information

Think about how much a criminal can learn from that combination. A Social Security number can help fuel identity theft. Banking information could put financial accounts at risk. Medical records can also give criminals deeply personal details that make phishing emails and scam calls far more convincing. Then there is another threat many people rarely think about: medical identity theft.
MEDICAL IDENTITY THEFT FOLLOWS YOU INTO THE DOCTOR'S OFFICE
Data breaches can expose far more than passwords, including Social Security numbers, financial details and deeply personal health information. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
Why stolen medical information can follow you for years

You can change a password after a breach. Your medical history is much harder to replace. A criminal could use stolen insurance or personal information to seek medical care under someone else's identity. Fraudulent claims can also appear under a victim's health insurance.

In some cases, incorrect treatment or medical information could eventually make its way into someone's records. That creates problems that can extend beyond financial fraud. The Federal Trade Commission advises people who suspect medical identity theft to review their medical records and insurance statements. Look closely for unfamiliar treatments, providers, prescriptions or charges. We recently covered this growing problem in Medical identity theft follows you into the doctor's office.
What CareCloud says happened after the attack

CareCloud says it brought in outside cybersecurity specialists after discovering the incident. The company also reported the attack to law enforcement and secured the affected environment. According to its breach notice, investigators found no continued unauthorized access after the incident was contained.

CareCloud has also offered affected individuals complimentary identity protection services through IDX. If you received a notification letter, check it carefully for enrollment instructions and the amount of time you have to sign up.
CyberGuy reached out to CareCloud for comment, but we did not hear back before our deadline.
After a healthcare breach, watching your accounts, protecting your devices and staying alert for convincing scams can help reduce the risk of further damage. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
How to protect yourself after the CareCloud data breach

A breach involving Social Security numbers, medical records and financial information deserves your attention even if you have not noticed anything suspicious yet. Here are the steps I recommend taking.

Start with the letter or notification you received. Look for the specific types of information CareCloud says were involved in your case. Not every affected person necessarily had the same information exposed. If you were offered free identity protection or credit monitoring, review the terms and enrollment deadline. Consider signing up while the service remains available.

If your Social Security number was exposed, consider freezing your credit with Equifax, Experian and TransUnion. A credit freeze limits access to your credit file. That can stop many criminals from opening new credit accounts in your name. Federal law allows you to freeze and unfreeze your credit for free. However, a credit freeze cannot block every form of identity theft. Someone could still attempt to take over an existing account or misuse your personal information in other ways. For a deeper look at those limitations, read Why a credit freeze isn't the end of identity theft.

Keep an eye on your bank accounts, credit cards and credit reports. Look for purchases you do not recognize, unfamiliar credit inquiries or accounts you never opened. If something looks suspicious, contact the bank or financial institution directly. Use the phone number printed on your card or listed on the company's official website. Be wary of anyone who unexpectedly contacts you and claims they need personal information to investigate the CareCloud breach.

Do not limit your monitoring to your credit report. Sign in to your healthcare portals and review your records. Also look carefully at the explanation of benefits statements from your health insurer. Watch for unfamiliar doctors, procedures you never received or claims that make no sense. If something looks wrong, contact both your healthcare provider and insurer. Medical identity fraud may never trigger a traditional credit alert, which makes checking these records particularly important.

Use strong and unique passwords for important accounts, especially email, banking and healthcare services. If you reuse the same password on multiple sites, change it. A password manager can generate and securely store complex passwords so you do not have to remember them all. Turn on two-factor authentication (2FA) whenever it is available. That extra verification step can make it harder for someone to get into an account even if they obtain your password. Pay extra attention to your primary email account. Criminals can use access to your inbox to reset passwords for other services.

A stolen medical record could give a scammer enough personal information to send you a very convincing message. You might receive an email that appears to come from a doctor, health insurer or breach-response company. The message could include a malicious attachment or direct you to a fake login page. Strong antivirus software can help detect malicious links, dangerous downloads and other threats that arrive through phishing emails or scam messages. The best way to safeguard yourself from malicious links that install malware, potentially accessing your private information, is to have strong antivirus software installed on all your devices. This protection can also alert you to phishing emails and ransomware scams, helping keep your personal information and digital assets safer. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android & iOS devices at Cyberguy.com

This breach creates another problem. Scammers may now have enough real information about victims to sound believable. Be skeptical if someone suddenly contacts you claiming to represent CareCloud, your doctor, your insurance company or a credit-monitoring service. A criminal might know your name, address or other personal details. That knowledge does not make the person contacting you legitimate. Avoid clicking links in unexpected messages. Instead, open the organization's official website yourself or call a number you already trust. Also be suspicious of anyone demanding immediate payment or asking you to provide a verification code.

The information stolen from CareCloud can become even more useful to criminals when they combine it with data that already appears online. People-search websites and data brokers can contain your phone number, current or previous addresses and other identifying information. Scammers can combine those details with breached data to build a more complete profile of you. A personal data removal service can help reduce your online footprint by sending removal requests to data brokers on your behalf. Some services also continue checking to see whether your information reappears. No service can guarantee that every piece of personal information will disappear from the internet. Still, removing information from data broker databases can make it harder for scammers to gather additional details about you. You can make removal requests yourself as well. However, doing it manually can be time-consuming and may require repeated requests. Check out my top picks for data removal services and get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web by visiting Cyberguy.com

If you discover that someone is using your information, act quickly. Visit the Federal Trade Commission's IdentityTheft.gov website to report identity theft and create a personalized recovery plan. Keep records of suspicious transactions, emails and letters related to the fraud. Save copies of any reports you file as well. The sooner you spot suspicious activity, the sooner you can start limiting the damage.
Kurt's key takeaways

What bothers me most about the CareCloud breach is how little control you may have over where your medical information ends up. You can choose a doctor you trust. You can create strong passwords and protect your own devices. Yet some of your most sensitive information may still pass through another company's systems behind the scenes. That leaves millions of people dealing with the consequences when something goes wrong. If your information was involved, I would take the notification seriously even if everything looks normal today. A stolen Social Security number or medical record can remain useful to criminals long after the original breach fades from the news. Freeze your credit if your Social Security number was exposed. Watch your medical records and financial accounts over time. Then be especially cautious when an unexpected email, call or text seems to know surprisingly personal details about you. I would also reduce what data brokers can easily find about you and keep strong antivirus protection running on your devices. Those added layers can make follow-up attacks harder for scammers to pull off.

title: Patrick Clancy speaks out after hung jury in Lindsay Clancy case, addresses prospect of another trial
summary: Patrick Clancy says enduring another trial would be "extraordinarily painful" after a hung jury led to a mistrial in Lindsay Clancy's murder case.
story: The Lindsay Clancy case ends in a mistrial and legal experts analyze potential next steps. Harvard Law Professor Emeritus Alan Dershowitz weighs in on the defense's strategy.

Patrick Clancy broke his silence after a mistrial was declared in Lindsay Clancy’s case, saying the prospect of enduring another trial over the killings of their three children is "extraordinarily painful."

"Patrick Clancy is grateful to the Court and to the jurors for their hard work, their commitment, and their perseverance. The loss of Patrick’s children is something from which he will never recover and from which there will never be closure," his attorney, David Meier, wrote in a statement issued on Patrick's behalf.
"The prospect of reliving this tragedy through another trial is extraordinarily painful — for Patrick, for his family, and for all us," the statement concluded.

Patrick Clancy has previously asked the public to forgive his ex-wife, who has admitted killing their three children — 5-year-old Cora, 3-year-old Dawson and 8-month-old Callan. Her attorneys have argued she was legally insane due to postpartum psychosis.
LINDSAY CLANCY'S EX-HUSBAND HAS QUIETLY REMARRIED AND STARTED OVER AMID HER MURDER TRIAL
Patrick Clancy on the stand at Lindsay Clancy's murder trial on July 29, 2026. (David L. Ryan/The Boston Globe via Getty Images)

During the trial, Patrick Clancy testified about the day of the killings on Jan. 24, 2023. The children were killed while he was running errands that included picking up children's stool softener at a CVS store and takeout for dinner. They spoke on the phone while he was out.

On Friday afternoon, Judge William Sullivan declared a mistrial in the high-profile murder case after jurors said they were unable to reach a unanimous verdict. It will now be up to prosecutors whether Clancy will be tried again.
The jury spent a week deliberating at Plymouth Superior Court in Plymouth, Massachusetts, where supporters and onlookers gathered outside for days awaiting a possible verdict.

The mistrial followed an alleged 11-1 divide among jurors, with Clancy’s defense arguing that the lone holdout juror had acknowledged doubt but was refusing to properly apply the court’s instructions on reasonable doubt.

Lindsay Clancy looks on as jurors enter the courtroom during Clancy's murder trial at the Plymouth County Superior Court in Plymouth, Massachusetts, on Sept. 4, 2026. (Greg Derr / POOL / AFP via Getty Images)
LINDSAY CLANCY’S EX-HUSBAND DETAILS ‘BIG SPIRAL’ AS EXPERT SAYS ONE PART ‘SCARED ME’ IN MOM’S MURDER TRIAL
The alleged holdout is believed to be one of the three male jurors. Defense attorney Kevin Reddington repeatedly referred to the unnamed juror as a male inside and outside court.
Clancy’s attorneys made an emergency appeal to the Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court in an attempt to stay the mistrial and force further inquiry into the juror.

Judge William Sullivan declared a mistrial Lindsay Clancy's murder trial after the jury in the case were unable to reach a verdict on Sept. 4, 2026, in Plymouth, Mass. (Greg Derr/The Patriot Ledger via AP, Pool)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Justice Dalila Argaez Wendlandt denied the request Friday afternoon, and shortly after, Sullivan declared a mistrial.

Sullivan said he wants the case retried "sooner rather than later,", suggesting a new trial could potentially take place later this fall. Clancy is due back in court Sept. 29 for a status hearing, trial assignment and a defense Rule 25 motion.

title: ‘Black widow’ allegedly attempted to murder romantic partner, 69, she met online
summary: Samantha Adams allegedly slipped benzodiazepines into a drink she gave the 69-year-old victim she met on a dating app, Polk County sheriff says.
story: Deputies are calling an Orlando woman a "black widow." The Polk County Sheriff's Office is accusing a woman of trying to poison a man she met online. (FOX 13)
A Florida woman is behind bars and facing an attempted murder charge after she allegedly drugged a man she’d met on a dating app.
Samantha Adams, 39, and the victim, 69, had been in a relationship "for the purposes of…paid sex" for two to three months after meeting online, said Polk County Sheriff Grady Judd.
Adams had told the victim her name was "Nala."
"Black widow" is what Polk County deputies call her, Judd said.
FLORIDA MAN WHO ALLEGEDLY LURED WOMEN WITH DATING APP COULD HAVE MORE VICTIMS: AUTHORITIES

Samantha Adams, 39, faces an attempted murder charge after investigators say an elderly romantic partner suffered benzodiazepine poisoning following a meeting at his home. (Polk County Sheriff’s Office)
"She tried to kill him," Judd said in a video posted to social media. "She tried to overdose him. She tried to extort him."

On Aug. 17, Adams and the victim were in an argument about a vehicle he’d bought for her, court records show. When he told her he wanted it back because he couldn’t afford it, she said they could discuss it at his house, according to records.
When at the victim’s home, Adams gave him a shot glass filled with "suspected whiskey," court records show.
"She slipped him benzodiazepine," Judd said.

After he drank the beverage, the two "engaged in physical affection," court records show. When the victim "attempted to touch the defendant in a sexual manner," Adams demanded $1,000, according to court records. When he told her he didn't have the money, she got dressed and left the home.
MIAMI WOMAN ALLEGEDLY LURED MAN TO LUXURY CONDO VIA INSTAGRAM, THEN ROBBED HIM WITH 2 ACCOMPLICES
Not long after, the victim was asked to pick up his granddaughter from a Wawa gas station near a movie theater where he’d dropped her off with her boyfriend earlier that day.
On his way to the Wawa, he began feeling ill, court records show.
Later, he could only recall being pulled from the driver's seat by his granddaughter and being moved to the back seat of the vehicle, Adams’ arrest warrant shows.
Polk County Sheriff Grady Judd says Samantha Adams allegedly drugged and tried to extort a 69-year-old man she met through online dating. (Carmen Whitehead via Getty Images)
The granddaughter drove her unconscious grandfather home. When he was still unconscious later in the evening, she called 911.
At the hospital, the victim was given Narcan for a suspected opioid overdose, records show.
A urine analysis and other testing showed he had benzodiazepine poisoning, metabolic encephalopathy, dehydration, and acute kidney injury, investigators reported.
PEOPLE TAKING COMMON SLEEP DRUG MAY NOT REALIZE THEY'RE TOO IMPAIRED TO DRIVE, STUDY FINDS

Benzodiazepines are depressants that cause sedation and hypnosis, according to the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration. Overdosing on the drug can cause extreme drowsiness, confusion, impaired coordination, decreased reflexes, respiratory depression, coma and possible death.
The victim told investigators that he doesn’t drink often.
The last time he drank and consumed "exponentially higher" amounts of alcohol was on the Fourth of July, when he had three Long Island Teas and three beers, he said.
And he was never drowsy and disoriented like he was when he drank with Adams, he told investigators. It wasn’t the first time the victim had become drowsy after meeting with Adams, he said.
FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X

Earlier in August, the victim fell asleep behind the wheel after leaving Adams’ home. He was awakened by an Osceola County Sheriff's deputy after he accidentally reversed his truck into the deputy's agency vehicle.
STEPDAD ACCUSED OF SEX ASSAULT AS COPS WIDEN PROBE INTO GIRL’S LETHAL BENADRYL INGREDIENT DOSE
"There's lots of investigations still to go," Judd said. "That’s underway."

The victim’s normal medications do not include benzodiazepines, investigators found.
Sheriff Grady Judd said Samantha Adams tried to kill the man she had met on a dating app. (REUTERS/Pierre DuCharme)
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE

He also was assessed for mental acuity and wasn’t found to be in a forgetful state of mind or a state in which he would intentionally take the drugs to hurt himself. And he wasn’t found to have a previous history of opioid use.
SEND US A TIP
Ten days after the incident, Adams was arrested outside of a Dick’s Sporting Goods in Polk County on Aug. 27.
GOT A TIP?
In addition to attempted murder, she’s been charged with resisting an officer without violence, offering prostitution, tampering with physical evidence and five different drug-related charges.
LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

When searching Adams’ vehicle, authorities found prescription medication including: 19 pills of hydrocodone/acetaminophen, 2 1⁄2 pills of oxycodone hydrochloride, nine Zoloft pills, a partial Adderall pill and a partial Xanax pill.

Adams was previously involved in a Lake County investigation in which a woman named "Nala" was approaching an elderly man "with the intent to obtain goods and money from the gentleman," court records show.

title: Charles Manson's 'Helter Skelter' motive a myth? New tapes reveal what may have sparked Sharon Tate murders
summary: Joe Berlinger's Netflix docuseries argues the Charles Manson murders were not about starting a race war but covering up a drug deal gone bad.
story: Anthony DiMaria, Jay Sebring's nephew, spoke about the late celebrity groomer's life and legacy. DiMaria teamed up with author Marshall Terrill to write "Jay Sebring: Cutting to the Truth."

For decades, the prevailing story of the Manson murders held that Charles Manson masterminded a murderous plot to ignite a race war inspired by the Beatles. But Joe Berlinger argues the infamous story never added up.

The true crime filmmaker directed a three-part Netflix docuseries titled "Conversations with a Killer: The Charles Manson Tapes." It features previously unreleased prison audio from the cult leader and some of his "Manson Family" members.

In 1969, the career criminal who surrounded himself with runaways and other lost souls directed his followers to commit a series of murders in and around Los Angeles. Prosecutors argued the killings were part of Manson's "Helter Skelter" plan to ignite a race war.
CHARLES MANSON'S GRANDDAUGHTER REVEALS MOMENT SHE DISCOVERED DARK FAMILY SECRET: 'IT WAS DEVASTATING'
Charles Manson is brought into the Los Angeles city jail under suspicion of having masterminded the Tate-LaBianca murders of August 1969. (Getty Images)
But after studying the previously unreleased recordings, Berlinger argues the murders were instead a desperate attempt to cover up "a series of blunders."

"This whole idea of starting a race war was a false idea," Berlinger told Fox News Digital. "He certainly believed a race war was coming, or at least that's what he told his followers to control them. But the murders, in particular the Tate and LaBianca murders, were an attempt to get associate Bobby Beausoleil out of prison. He told his followers, 'He's my friend. You guys owe me a favor. Let's get him out of prison.'"

Robert Kenneth Beausoleil, aka Bobby Beausoleil, talks with newsmen after the jury returned a verdict against him of first-degree murder in the torture slaying of musician Gary Hinman. Beausoleil, a former member of the Manson Family, claimed Charles Manson sent him to Hinman's house to force the musician to turn over $20,000, but that Manson delivered the death blows. (Bettmann Archive)

"The truth is I believe, and others believe, that if they had succeeded in this crazy idea of getting Bobby Beausoleil out of prison, I think Manson would’ve killed him because he was a liability," said Berlinger. "But listening to those tapes made the story come alive, not these crazy conspiracy theories and myths that turned Charles Manson into the most mythologized figure in the history of true crime."
"Conversations with a Killer: The Charles Manson Tapes," directed by Joe Berlinger (pictured here) is available for streaming. (Netflix)
Berlinger traces the chain of events that led to the murders to a botched drug deal.

According to the documentary, Manson invited members of the Straight Satans motorcycle club to Spahn Ranch to protect him from the Black Panthers, whom he feared, offering them access to his female followers in exchange.
Dianne Lake, seen here in the documentary, is the youngest former member of the notorious Charles Manson cult, known by the nickname "Snake." (Courtesy of Netflix)

"[Follower] Tex Watson tried to steal money from a drug dealer named Bernard ‘Lotsapoppa’ Crowe, who wants his money back," Berlinger explained. "Manson goes out there and doesn't intend to kill him, but thinks he killed him, a Black Panther."
FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X
Charles "Tex" Watson. Watson was convicted of murder for his part in the killings of Sharon Tate and others while a member of the "Manson Family." (Getty Images)
According to the documentary, Watson stole Crowe's money, prompting Crowe to threaten retaliation. Manson later shot Crowe and mistakenly believed he had killed him. Crowe was not a Black Panther.
A sign at the Spahn Movie Ranch, owned by American rancher George Spahn and residence of the Manson Family in Los Angeles County, California on Aug. 28, 1970. (Michael Ochs Archives/Getty Images)

"He goes back to Spahn Ranch and becomes paranoid that the Black Panthers are going to come after him. He becomes friends with Bobby, tells him to join the family and also to help protect the ranch. Bobby becomes tight with some bikers who were also invited to protect the ranch from the Black Panthers."
Despite the overwhelming evidence against him, Charles Manson maintained during his tumultuous trial in 1970 that he was innocent and that society itself was guilty. (Netflix)

But the motorcycle gang wanted more than just women. The documentary says Beausoleil brought them drugs he obtained from music teacher Gary Hinman. The bikers were unhappy with the quality of the supply, and Beausoleil was pressured to recover their money.
Three bikers talk together in Venice, California. The man in front wears gang colors referencing the Straight Satans motorcycle club. (Getty Images)
"Bobby tries to get his money back from Gary and can’t get it," said Berlinger.

According to court records, during the confrontation, Manson arrived at Hinman's home and slashed Hinman's face with a sword, cutting him from his left ear toward his chin. Over the course of about three days, Manson's followers tortured Hinman. Beausoleil later stabbed Hinman to death and wrote the words "Political Piggy" on a wall in Hinman's blood, along with an animal paw print intended to implicate the Black Panthers.
Susan Atkins sits at the defendant's table at the Santa Monica Courthouse during a hearing regarding the murder of music teacher Gary Hinman in Los Angeles, on June 25, 1970. (Getty Images)
"Gary Hinman is killed because Manson comes in, wields a sword and then tells Bobby 'finish the job' to cover the tracks," Berlinger said.

Robert "Bobby" Beausoleil poses for a mugshot after his arrest on Aug. 7, 1969. (Getty Images)
Beausoleil was arrested about a week after Hinman’s body was discovered. Berlinger said Beausoleil was driving Hinman’s vehicle and had "the murder weapon stupidly in the stolen car."

Berlinger said Manson wanted police to believe Hinman’s murder was the work of the Black Panthers to cast suspicion away from Beausoleil. He noted the attempt to free Beausoleil became the catalyst for the murders that followed.
Jay Sebring and Sharon Tate, circa 1966. (Michael Ochs Archives/Getty Images)

On Aug. 9, 1969, Manson's followers murdered five people at a Los Angeles home previously rented by music producer Terry Melcher: actress Sharon Tate, who was 8 1/2 months pregnant; coffee heiress Abigail Folger; celebrity hairstylist Jay Sebring; Polish writer Wojciech Frykowski; and Steven Parent, who had been visiting the estate's caretaker.
The five victims were found slain on August 9, 1969. From left: Woijech "Voytek" Frykowski, Sharon Tate, Steven Parent, Jay Sebring and Abigail Folger. (CPL Archives/Everett Collection)
Melcher had previously declined to sign Manson to a recording contract.

"The murder is tried to be made to look like it was part of Gary Hinman’s murder," said Berlinger. "But when Manson picks up the paper the next day, and there’s no information about these two murders being linked, they do another murder. The logic is, ‘We’ve got to make people think that Bobby, who is sitting in prison, is not guilty.’"

Charles Manson travels in a police van to the Santa Monica Courthouse to appear in court for a hearing regarding the murder of music teacher Gary Hinman in Los Angeles, California on June 25, 1970. (Michael Ochs Archives/Getty Images)
"This was all a series of blunders, a bunch of bad, spontaneous decision-making."
GET REAL-TIME UPDATES DIRECTLY ON THE TRUE CRIME HUB
A road sign marks Cielo Drive in Los Angeles, where actress Sharon Tate was murdered in 1969 during a series of killings orchestrated by Charles Manson. (Picture Alliance via Getty Images)

The next night, wealthy grocer Leno LaBianca and his wife, Rosemary LaBianca, were stabbed and killed in their home across town. The killers scrawled phrases including "Pigs" and the misspelled words "Healter Skelter" in blood at the crime scene.
Manson was arrested in October 1969.
Doris Day is seen here with her son Terry Melcher. (Ron Galella Collection via Getty Images)

Prosecutors maintained at trial that Manson ordered his followers to kill some of Los Angeles' rich and famous to trigger a race war, a plan prosecutors said grew in part from his interpretation of the Beatles' song "Helter Skelter."
Manson family members Susan Atkins, Patricia Krenwinkle and Leslie van Houton. (Bettmann Archive)

Manson frequently spoke about an impending race war and interpreted songs on the Beatles' "White Album" as messages about the coming conflict, according to testimony from his followers. What remains disputed is whether those beliefs motivated the Tate-LaBianca murders or whether, as Berlinger argues, prosecutors elevated them into the central theory of their case.

Deputy District Attorney Vincent Bugliosi talks to journalists outside the courtroom after the jury decreed the death penalty for Charles Manson and three female followers in the Tate-LaBianca murders of August 1969. (Bettmann Archive)

"[Prosecutor Vincent Bugliosi] had to come up with a legal theory to convict a guy who actually didn’t do the killings," Berlinger said. "Manson wasn’t even there when the Tate-LaBianca killings took place. So how do you convict somebody who wasn’t there? Well, you come up with this organizing principle that he convinced his followers that a race war was coming, and he was trying to make that race war happen. It was a brilliant legal theory, but it’s a false story."
"The Manson murders are much more tragic, but much more banal than this idea of some crazy cult trying to start a race war," Berlinger continued.

Charles Manson sits at the defendant's table at the Santa Monica Courthouse during a hearing regarding the murder of music teacher Gary Hinman in Los Angeles, on June 25, 1970. Manson follower Bobby Beausoleil murdered Hinman in July 1969, less than two weeks before the Tate-LaBianca killings. (Michael Ochs Archives/Getty Images)

"This was a drug deal gone bad, trying to cover up Gary Hinman’s killing by doing another murder the next day to make it look like a copycat murder, which were the Tate murders. And when that murder didn’t hit newspapers like a Black Panther murder, they did the LaBianca murders. It’s a series of blunders by people who were trying to cover their tracks, not this grand scheme of 'Helter Skelter.'"

Bugliosi worked with writer Curt Gentry on a book about the case. Published in 1974, "Helter Skelter" became the bestselling true crime book of all time.
The book "Helter Skelter" by Vincent Bugliosi and Curt Gentry, photographed on Jan. 10, 2014, in New York City. (Getty Images)

Manson and three followers — Susan Atkins, Patricia Krenwinkel and Leslie Van Houten — were found guilty and later sentenced to death. Charles "Tex" Watson was tried separately and convicted later. Their death sentences were reduced to life in prison after the California Supreme Court invalidated the state's death penalty in 1972.
Charles Manson's 1969 mugshot. (Getty Images)
Atkins died in prison in 2009. Van Houten was released on parole in 2023. Krenwinkel and Watson remain in prison.

Manson died at a California hospital in 2017 while serving a life sentence. He was 83.
LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST
According to Netflix, "Conversations with a Killer, The Charles Manson Tapes" features Manson’s final known recordings and documents his rise to notoriety. (Netflix)
GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL
Berlinger maintained Manson's reputation as an evil mastermind was fueled more by myth than reality.
SEND US A TIP

"He wasn’t killing or ordering people to kill to get some kind of satisfaction," Berlinger said. "He was covering up a series of blunders and just getting deeper and deeper into a hole. The best way to honor the victims is to be truthful about what happened."

title: ICE officer pleads not guilty to lying about Minneapolis shooting involving Venezuelan man
summary: Video evidence allegedly contradicted the ICE officer's claims about the Minneapolis shooting of Venezuelan man Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis, prosecutors say.
story: Fox News correspondent Christina Coleman reports from Dallas on a federal judge blocking attempts by Minnesota to extradite ICE agent Christian Castro from Texas. Castro faces charges stemming from the January shooting of a Venezuelan migrant during Operation Metro Surge in Minneapolis, while Texas Gov. Greg Abbott investigates whether the officer legally qualifies as a fugitive.

A U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer pleaded not guilty Friday to charges of lying about a January shooting of a Venezuelan man in Minneapolis during the Trump administration's crackdown on illegal immigration.

Christian Castro appeared in a Texas federal court where he faces six charges of making "materially false" statements to investigators, according to federal court documents unsealed Friday. He turned himself in to authorities Thursday evening.
A judge ordered Castro released on a $75,000 unsecured bond and required him to wear an ankle monitor.
DOJ CHARGES ICE OFFICER WITH LYING TO INVESTIGATORS FOLLOWING MINNEAPOLIS SHOOTING OF VENEZUELAN MAN

Left: Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer Christian Castro gets into a car surrounded by news reporters moments after being released from the Carrizalez-Rucker Cameron County Detention Center in Brownsville, Texas on Thursday, Aug. 27, 2026; Right: Christian Castro. (Left: AP Photo/Michael Gonzalez; Right: Cameron County Sheriff's Office)
The charges stem from the Jan. 14 shooting of Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis, a Venezuelan man who was shot in the leg. Moments earlier, Castro and his partner attempted to stop a vehicle.
The driver, also a Venezuelan citizen, fled, triggering a foot chase.

Castro caught up to the driver and a physical struggle ensued, according to the indictment. Sosa-Celis attempted to help the driver, and they both fled into a nearby apartment duplex and shut the door.
ICE AGENTS IN FATAL HOUSTON SHOOTING WERE NOT WEARING BODY CAMERAS, SOURCES SAY
Castro drew his service weapon and fired a single shot through the front door, striking Sosa-Celis in the leg, federal prosecutors said.
Two 1-year-old children and two women were inside the home when Castro opened fire, prosecutors added.

In an attempt to justify the shooting, Castro allegedly told investigators he was brutally assaulted by multiple individuals wielding tools, claiming he was hit with a broom and a snow shovel during the confrontation. He also claimed he was on his back when he fired toward the fleeing men, officials said.
TRUMP ADMINISTRATION HAS LOST OR ABANDONED HUNDREDS OF LAWSUITS AGAINST ANTI-ICE PROTESTERS, MIGRANTS: REPORT
FILE - U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents conduct immigration enforcement operations in Minneapolis, Minnesota, on Thursday, Jan. 28, 2026. (Madison Thorn/Anadolu via Getty Images)

However, video evidence later contradicted those statements, prompting an investigation. Federal prosecutors said Castro was standing up when he opened fire, and they disputed his claim that he fought the suspect on the ground for three minutes, noting the struggle actually lasted about 11 seconds.
The shooting occurred amid a targeted crackdown on illegal immigration in Minneapolis.
Castro faces separate charges in Minnesota and was previously arrested in Texas in May.
ICE OFFICER CHARGED IN MINNEAPOLIS SHOOTING RELEASED IN TEXAS AFTER JUDGE DECLINES TO INTERVENE

His case has sparked a legal battle involving Texas Gov. Greg Abbott, who has refused to extradite him to Minnesota.

title: Illinois mother charged with murder in death of 2-year-old son in case drawing comparisons to Lindsay Clancy
summary: Corie Walsh faces three murder charges in her 2-year-old son's death, a Frankfort, Illinois, case that a neighbor says mirrors the Lindsay Clancy trial.
story: Constitutional law attorney Jonathan Turley discusses Plymouth County Superior Court Judge William Sullivan declaring a mistrial in the Lindsay Clancy case after the jury remained deadlocked and the Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court denied the defense's emergency appeal, breaking down the legal implications of the ruling, the prosecution's options moving forward and what to expect if the case heads to a second trial on 'America Reports.'
An Illinois woman has been charged with three counts of murder in the death of her 2-year-old son in a case that has already drawn comparisons to the Lindsay Clancy trial, authorities confirmed.

Corie A. Walsh, 40, was being held for medical treatment on Friday after she was found with wounds believed to be self-inflicted but non-life-threatening when police responded to her home Tuesday, the Frankfort Police Department said in a news release.
Frankfort is about 36 miles southwest of Chicago.
SOCIAL MEDIA IS LINDSAY CLANCY WILD CARD THAT COULD TILT POTENTIAL RETRIAL TO THE DEFENSE, RETIRED JUDGE SAYS
An investigator works behind police tape outside a Frankfort, Ill., home where a 2-year-old boy died. (FOX 32 Chicago)
Once she’s released from treatment, she will be transferred to the Will County Adult Detention Facility to await a hearing.
Frankfort police officers responded to Walsh’s home Tuesday afternoon and found her son unresponsive. He was given CPR and transported to a hospital where he was later pronounced dead.
Walsh was closely following the Clancy trial and was discussing the case in an online group chat as the jury deliberated just hours before her son was found, prosecutors said, according to FOX 32.
Walsh allegedly believed her son was the "anti-Christ" and the "devil," court documents said, the station reported.
The boy was found by a neighbor hanging by the neck from a rafter in the basement, FOX 32 reported.
Fox News Digital has reached out to the Will County State's Attorney's Office and the Frankfort Police Department.
NORTH DAKOTA MOM STABS HER 2 CHILDREN TO DEATH IN 'HORRIFIC' KILLING THAT LEFT COPS TRAUMATIZED: OFFICIALS

"Our thoughts and prayers are with the family, their loved ones and everyone affected by this heartbreaking tragedy," Frankfort police said in a statement shared with Fox News Digital. Lindsay Clancy listens to testimony at Plymouth Superior Court in Plymouth, Mass., last month. (Boston Globe via Getty Images)
LINDSAY CLANCY’S FUTURE COULD REST WITH ‘PROSECUTION DOCTORS’ AS CASE ECHOES INFAMOUS MAINE KILLINGS: EXPERT

Carolyn Pappas, who lives nearby, told NBC Chicago earlier this week that the boy’s death has left residents stunned. "This is just absolutely devastating, that this could be another Lindsay Clancy situation in our neighborhood, in our community. Police tape surrounds the Frankfort, Illinois, home where officers found an unresponsive 2-year-old boy. (Fox 32 Chicago)

title: First responders honor World Trade Center beam arriving at Boston fallen heroes memorial
summary: The Tunnel to Towers Steel Across America tour brought a 21-foot World Trade Center beam to the Massachusetts Fallen Heroes Memorial in Boston.
story: The Tunnel to Towers tour made a stop in Boston with a section of World Trade Center steel.
The Tunnel to Towers Steel Across America tour honored fallen heroes in Boston Wednesday as part of a nationwide tour slated to finish in New York City just after Sept. 11.
The group brought a preserved 21-foot steel beam from the South Tower of the World Trade Center, which has been on tour since May, to the Massachusetts Fallen Heroes Memorial in Boston's Seaport.

"For us as first responders and veterans, what this means as we come up on the 25th anniversary is personal. It's all about educating the next generation and not forgetting the sacrifices, not only made on 9/11 but what we've endured in the 20 years after in all theaters of combat," said Dan Magoon, executive director of Massachusetts Fallen Heroes.
AMERICA’S HEARTLAND COMES FACE-TO-FACE WITH 9/11 HISTORY AS 25TH ANNIVERSARY NEARS

Guests pay their respects Wednesday as they approach a 21-foot, 16,900-pound steel beam recovered from the World Trade Center's South Tower during the Steel Across America tour at the Massachusetts Fallen Heroes Memorial in Boston's Seaport. (Jason Thiele Fotografik Memories)

Mike Eruzione, captain of the 1980 U.S. Winter Olympics hockey team that won the historic "Miracle on Ice" game against the Soviet Union, honored his friends who were passengers on one of the hijacked planes involved in the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks.

"It touched the heart of our country. It touched the souls of our country," Eruzione said of Tunnel to Towers, which helps 9/11 families, first responders and veterans rebuild in part from funds raised through nationwide charity runs.
FRANK SILLER: 'I LOVE YOU, BROTHER' — THE 9/11 LOSS THAT INSPIRED A MISSION OF SERVICE
Guests stand in front of the Massachusetts Fallen Heroes Memorial in Boston Wednesday. (Jason Thiele Fotografik Memories)
The gathering brought together first responders from Massachusetts as well as law enforcement. Guests were allowed to approach the 16,900-pound beam and pay their respects.

"It's just crazy to think about where it once stood, the people that worked inside the buildings, the people that rushed inside to save those people and what happened when it all came down," said Daniel McCarthy, a Bostonian whose parents are from New York.
WHERE TUNNEL TO TOWERS' STEEL ACROSS AMERICA TOUR WILL STOP AHEAD OF 9/11
American flags on a grassy area at the Massachusetts Fallen Heroes Memorial in Boston. (Jason Thiele Fotografik Memories)
The beam was brought to Fenway Park Wednesday night after traveling to the U.S. Military Academy at West Point Monday.

title: Lindsay Clancy mistrial declared after jury deadlocks in killings of her three children
summary: Lindsay Clancy's trial centered on whether severe mental illness relieved her of criminal responsibility in the January 2023 deaths of her three children.
story: Plymouth County Superior Court Judge William Sullivan declares a mistrial in the Lindsay Clancy case after the jury deadlocked and a defense appeal was denied.

Judge William Sullivan declared a mistrial Friday in Lindsay Clancy’s murder case after jurors said they were unable to reach a unanimous verdict in the killings of her three children after a week of deliberating at the Plymouth Superior Court in Plymouth, Massachusetts.

The mistrial followed a dramatic dispute over an alleged 11-1 divide, with Clancy’s defense arguing that the lone holdout juror had acknowledged doubt but was refusing to properly apply the court’s instructions on reasonable doubt.

The alleged holdout is believed to be one of the three male jurors on the 12-person panel after defense attorney Kevin Reddington repeatedly referred to the unnamed juror as a male inside and outside court.
POSTPARTUM MOM LINDSAY CLANCY ON TRIAL FOR MURDER BRINGS COURT TO A HALT WITH SUDDEN BREAKDOWN

"[The other jurors] know that they were robbed — by one man — for whatever his agenda was, who stole seven weeks of the life of these other jurors that were so attentive, so beautiful, so wonderful and listened to this evidence," he told reporters after leaving the courthouse.
"And you could see how defeated they were sitting there. And I got a funny feeling they could go one for another week if they had to. So, I hope that guy can sleep well at night."
Callan, Dawson and Cora Clancy. The three children were killed at their Duxbury, Mass., home in January 2023. (Lindsay Marie Clancy/Facebook)

Also speaking outside the courthouse, Plymouth County District Attorney Tim Cruz acknowledged the victims in this case — the Clancy children: 5-year-old Cora, 3-year-old Dawson and 8-month-old Callan.
"It is our job to make sure the victims are not invisible," Cruz said. "I am a father and a grandfather, and I cannot imagine the hell this entire family has lived through."

Clancy’s attorneys made an emergency appeal to the Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court in an attempt to stay the mistrial and force further inquiry into the juror. Justice Dalila Argaez Wendlandt denied the request Friday afternoon, clearing the way for Sullivan to formally declare the mistrial.
HEATED LINDSAY CLANCY COURTROOM EXCHANGE OVER 911 CALL, CRIME SCENE PHOTOS SETS STAGE FOR MOM’S MURDER TRIAL
Clancy had been charged with first-degree murder in the January 2023 deaths of her children, each of whom had been strangled with exercise bands.
The trial centered on whether she was legally responsible for her actions at the time, and the defense argued she wasn't due to postpartum psychosis.
Her attorneys argued that severe mental illness left her unable to appreciate the wrongfulness of what she was doing or unable to conform her conduct to the requirements of the law.
LINDSAY CLANCY’S HUSBAND COULD TESTIFY FOR HER AT TRIAL OVER DEATHS OF THEIR THREE CHILDREN
Lindsay and Patrick Clancy with two of their three children in an undated photo (Lindsay Marie Clancy/ Facebook)

Prosecutors maintained that Clancy remained criminally responsible and pointed to evidence they said showed planning, purposeful behavior and an awareness of what she was doing before, during and after the killings.

During the trial, Clancy's former husband, Patrick Clancy, testified about the day of the slayings, which happened while he was running errands that included picking up children's stool softener at a CVS store and takeout for dinner. They spoke on the phone while he was out.
Under Massachusetts law, once lack of criminal responsibility is properly raised, prosecutors must prove beyond a reasonable doubt that a defendant was criminally responsible.
Lindsay and Patrick Clancy with two of their three children in an undated photo (Lindsay Marie Clancy/Facebook)
The mistrial means the case ended without a verdict, and Clancy was neither convicted nor acquitted. Prosecutors can seek to retry her but have not yet announced a decision.

Sullivan said he wants the case retried "sooner rather than later," suggesting a new trial could potentially take place later this fall. Clancy is due back in court Sept. 29 for a status hearing, trial assignment and a defense Rule 25 motion.
All previous bail orders remain in effect.
JUDGE SENTENCES NEVADA MOM FOR DROWNING YOUNG SON, DAUGHTER: 'I WILL REMEMBER YOUR CASE FOREVER'
Lindsay Clancy listens to testimony Aug. 10, 2026. (Greg Derr/Pool/The Patriot Ledger)
FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X
The mistrial followed a trial that focused extensively on Clancy's psychiatric condition in the months and weeks before the children died.
Lindsay Clancy holding her youngest child, Callan, who was only 7 months old when he died.  (Lindsay Marie Clancy Facebook)
Jurors heard testimony about her treatment by mental health professionals, psychiatric medications, anxiety, depression, insomnia and other symptoms documented before the killings.

Attorney Kevin Reddington holds up a display board of a text message Lindsay Clancy sent her mother Paula during her murder trial in Plymouth Superior Court Aug. 26, 2026, in Plymouth, Mass. (Greg Derr/The Patriot Ledger/Pool via AP)
On Jan. 24, 2023, authorities responded to the Clancy family's Duxbury home after Patrick Clancy returned and found his wife seriously injured outside the house.

The couple's three children were found inside.
BROOKLYN MOTHER WHO DROWNED HER THREE CHILDREN IN THE OCEAN NEAR CONEY ISLAND SENTENCED TO DECADES IN PRISON

Prosecutor Jennifer Sprague rested her case as defense attorney Kevin Reddington asked rebuttal witness Dr. Gregory Saathoff one last question during the Lindsay Clancy murder trial at Plymouth Superior Court in Plymouth, Mass., Aug. 26, 2026. (Greg Derr/Pool The Patriot Ledger via AP)
Cora and Dawson died that night. Callan was taken to a hospital and died several days later.
Lindsay Clancy survived after jumping from a second-story window and suffered injuries that left her paralyzed in a wheelchair.
The prosecution and defense offered sharply different explanations for what happened before the children were killed.
Patrick Clancy and Rachel Danis hold hands as they walk through East Midtown in New York City, N.Y. Sept. 2, 2026.  (Elder Ordonez/InStar for Fox News Digital)

The defense had argued that the deaths occurred after months of worsening psychiatric symptoms and treatment and that Clancy's mental condition had deteriorated to the point she could not legally be held criminally responsible.

Specifically, the defense contended that Clancy heard a male voice that commanded her to kill her three children. Dr. Phillip Resnick, a forensic psychiatrist, said it was almost as if she was a "puppet."

"Not only did she hear a command, but she felt that her body was taken over by an external force where she was in a dream state and did not have control of her own body. It was almost like she was a puppet, and someone else was pulling the strings," Resnick said.
However, prosecutors rejected that claim, and their experts argued Clancy deliberately created an opportunity to be alone with the children and intentionally killed them.

Lindsay Clancy listens to the testimony of Dr. Gregory Saathoff during her murder trial in Plymouth Superior Court Aug. 26, 2026 in Plymouth, Mass. (Greg Derr/The Patriot Ledger via AP, Pool)

Gregory Saathoff, a forensic psychiatrist at the University of Virginia who consults the FBI's Behavioral Analysis Unit, told jurors Clancy's self-described auditory hallucinations were "very unusual."

"What was significant to me is that she had not spoken about hearing voices before to any of the mental health professionals, psychiatrists, nurse practitioners, physicians and staff in the emergency department or at McLean," Saathoff said.

"This was the first time she reported that, and that she experienced an auditory hallucination, according to what she told me. So, that was unusual. And then what was very unusual was the fact that the voice stopped with the strangling of her youngest son."
During the trial, members of Clancy's family revealed they were "very concerned" about her mental health in the months before she killed her three kids.
Susan Clancy, Lindsay's mother-in-law, told jurors she was concerned about Lindsay's mental health during the holiday season in 2022 but said she was a caring mother.
"Lindsay was struggling. We were all very concerned," Susan Clancy said. "She was very nurturing, very loving. She was a wonderful mother. Wonderful.
"She was begging for help."

Susan Clancy, the former mother-in-law of Lindsay Clancy, testifies during Lindsay Clancy's murder trial in Plymouth Mass., Aug. 18, 2026 in Plymouth, Mass. (Jonathan Wiggs/The Boston Globe via AP, Pool)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Paula Musgrove, Lindsay Clancy's mother, also told jurors about the mental health problems. In an Oct. 20, 2022 text message, Lindsay Clancy asked her mother for help.

"Mom, will you please come up and stay with me for a bit? I'm really sick. Something is wrong. I had horrible insomnia all night, and I just don’t know how I am going to get through the day. ... It’s just really scary, and I don’t want to be alone," the text read.
Fox News' Michelle Langer and Maria Paronich contributed to this report.

title: West Virginia principal suspended after recording devices found in girls’ locker rooms
summary: The Brooke County principal faces two felony charges and is being held on $100,000 bond after officials reportedly found devices at the school and his home.

School administrators immediately suspended a West Virginia high school principal Wednesday after officials reportedly discovered recording devices placed in multiple locker rooms.

title: Former North Texas police officer given three life sentences for child pornography, solicitation of minor
summary: A North Texas jury convicted Daniel Joseph Bates after he claimed 300-plus explicit child images were part of a secret human trafficking investigation.
story: Collin County District Attorney Greg Willis and prosecutor Bill Wirksye react to Karmelo Anthony's 35-year murder sentence, emphasizing the jury's focus on evidence. They clarify jury selection, discuss the community's response and address Anthony's appeal, underscoring that the case was never about race despite outside narratives.

A former police officer in North Texas was ordered to serve three consecutive life sentences in prison after investigators found him in possession of over 300 videos and images of children being sexually abused, according to a statement from Johnson and Somerville Counties' district attorney.

Former Itasca Police Department Officer Daniel Joseph Bates was convicted Wednesday of possession of child pornography and online solicitation of a minor after a civilian set him up in an entrapment scheme, according to a statement District Attorney Timothy Good shared with Fox News Digital.
Texas Rangers arrested Bates after an adult decoy posing as a 15-year-old girl alerted police that Bates was communicating with someone he believed to be a minor, according to the statement.

The civilian alerted police to Bates' communications with him, prompting Rangers to obtain a search warrant for his digital devices, and they allegedly found over 300 images of minor children being sexually abused, according to the statement.
NEW MISSISSIPPI LAW EXPANDS DEATH PENALTY TO INCLUDE INMATES ON CHILD SEXUAL BATTERY CONVICTIONS

Daniel Joseph Bates, who was convicted Wednesday Sept. 2, 2026, of possession of child pornography and online solicitation of a minor. (Office of the District Attorney Timothy M. Good Johnson & Somervell Counties)

"The images and videos that had to be processed and presented to the jury are indescribable in the level of depravity they depict and the degree of deviance of the defendant who voluntarily possessed and viewed those types of images," Good said in the statement."

"Daniel Bates disgraced his badge and violated his oath and became the monster that he was sworn to protect the community from. Our community is safer with Bates serving three consecutive life sentences."
Johnson & Somervell Counties District Attorney Timothy M. Good, who prosecuted Bates' case. (Office of the District Attorney Timothy M. Good Johnson & Somervell Counties)
Bates testified that the child pornography in his possession was part of a secret investigation he was conducting into human traffickers, but prosecutors disputed that.
Bates was only a reserve police officer and, at the time of his arrest, was working highway construction security, according to authorities.
"Bates was unable to substantiate his claims that he was conducting an official police investigation," the statement read.
OHIO POLICE CHIEF ARRESTED IN FLORIDA AFTER GRAND JURY HANDS DOWN 70-COUNT CHILD SEX INDICTMENT

Bates reportedly told the person he was communicating with that, because he was a police officer, he carries a gun at all times. This prompted Arlind Queriman, a civilian who creates video content in which he exposes people who try to solicit minors for sex, to contact authorities, according to FOX 4 Dallas.

title: ICE lodges detainer for illegal immigrant charged in wrong-way Maryland crash that killed mom, daughter
summary: ICE lodged a detainer for Jose Antonio Caballero-Nolasco, an El Salvador immigrant charged with killing a mother and daughter in a wrong-way crash.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

FIRST ON FOX: An illegal immigrant from El Salvador charged with killing a mother and her daughter while driving drunk the wrong way on a Maryland freeway is being sought by federal immigration authorities.

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) has lodged a detainer request with authorities in Montgomery County for Jose Antonio Caballero-Nolasco, the Department of Homeland Security told Fox News Digital.
He is charged with two counts of grossly negligent manslaughter, two counts of homicide by motor vehicle while impaired by alcohol, and life-threatening injury by a motor vehicle.
ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT SUSPECT CHARGED IN CRASH THAT KILLED POLICE OFFICER AND HIS GIRLFRIEND
Split of Interstate 270 and Jose Antonio Caballero-Nolasco. (DHS; Sarah L. Voisin/The Washington Post via Getty Images)
ILLEGAL ALIEN CHARGED WITH KILLING 4 YOUNG PEOPLE IN WRONG-WAY DUI CRASH ON OKLAHOMA HIGHWAY
Officials said Caballero-Nolasco was under the influence while driving the wrong way on Interstate 270 on Aug. 29, right before he crashed head-on into a vehicle with four people inside.

Two of the occupants, Musammat Shamima Begum, 46, and her 23-year-old daughter Areebah Jahin, were killed. They were from Northern Virginia and were on their way home at the time of the crash, affiliate FOX 5 D.C. reported.
Two others, a 62-year-old man and an 8-year-old girl, survived and were taken to local hospitals.
Investigators said they believe that alcohol impairment was a contributing factor in the crash.
FILE - DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin said the tragedy was "completely avoidable." (Jim Lo Scalzo/EPA/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
ICE ARRESTS RELEASED ILLEGAL ALIEN ACCUSED OF KILLING DAUGHTER, 9, IN ARIZONA ROLLOVER CRASH

"This tragedy was completely avoidable. Musammat Shamima Begum and Areebah Jahin should still be alive. ICE has lodged a detainer asking officials in Maryland to commit to not releasing this killer back onto our streets," said DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin. "My thoughts and prayers are with the victims and their family, and for a swift recovery for those who were injured."

Responding officers at the scene of the crash said Caballero-Nolasco smelled of alcohol, had bloodshot eyes, and slurred speech after the crash. He did not show any signs of braking before the crash, FOX 5 reported.

"There were some beer bottles that he admitted that he had been drinking," said Montgomery County State’s Attorney John McCarthy. "There were other bottles that were empty and full bottles were found within the vehicle."

Caballero-Nolasco was taken to a local hospital before being transferred to the Montgomery County Detention Center.

title: Rock concert at Virginia's Wolf Trap canceled after worker is crushed to death beneath tour bus
summary: A tour bus support apparatus failed at Wolf Trap National Park, crushing a worker underneath, hours before Squeeze was set to perform Thursday.
story: A rock show at the Wolf Trap performing arts venue was canceled after a man was crushed by the tour bus he was working underneath.
A rock performance at a venue in Virginia was canceled Thursday after a man working on a tour bus in a nearby parking lot was crushed underneath it hours before the show, according to authorities.
U.S. Park Police told FOX 5 DC they responded to the Wolf Trap National Park for the Performing Arts at 5 p.m.
The English rock band "Squeeze" was scheduled to perform at 7:30 p.m. that night.
The worker was under the tour bus when officers arrived. Park Police said a supporting apparatus failed, causing the bus to come down on him.

"There was an accident involving a member of the community at Wolf Trap National Park," the venue said in a social media post. "Out of respect, tonight's show has been canceled."

"Squeeze are deeply saddened and shocked by an incident that occurred at the venue earlier today, which resulted in the loss of a life," the band said in a statement to Rolling Stone. "We will work with the promoter and venue regarding the possibility of rescheduling the show and will communicate further information to ticket holders as soon as it is available. Our thoughts remain with everyone affected by this tragic event."
Simon Hanson and Glenn Tilbrook of Squeeze perform live on stage at Hard Rock Live in the Seminole Hard Rock Hotel & Casino Sept. 22, 2021, in Hollywood, Fla. (Johnny Louis/Getty Images)

title: Coast Guard recovers 47 bales of suspected marijuana worth $2.4M after intercepting go-fast vessel
summary: The U.S. Coast Guard Cutter Escanaba intercepted a suspicious go-fast vessel and recovered 47 bales of suspected marijuana worth over $2.4 million.
story: U.S. Southern Command video shows Marines and sailors interdicting and boarding a vessel allegedly used as a floating refueling station for the Los Choneros drug trafficking organization before U.S. forces sank it.
The U.S. Coast Guard recovered more than a ton of suspected marijuana worth over $2.4 million after crews intercepted a suspicious go-fast vessel during a patrol, military officials said.
Crews recovered 47 bales weighing a combined 2,082 pounds along the vessel's previous route, according to Joint Interagency Task Force South (JIATF-S).
Four people were detained in connection with the operation, JIATF-S said.
Officials said the seizure happened during a routine patrol after the crew of U.S. Coast Guard Cutter Escanaba detected "a suspicious go-fast vessel" and launched a boat crew to investigate.
