The U.S.-led "Board of Peace" proposal centers on a phased ceasefire, demilitarization of Gaza, Israeli troop withdrawal, Palestinian technocratic governance and international reconstruction efforts.
Reuters contributed to this report.
Anders Hagstrom is a reporter with Fox News Digital covering national politics and major breaking news events.

title: Trump says Iran is ‘DEAD’ — experts point to the real sign Tehran is nearing the brink
summary: U.S. strikes on Iranian launchers near the Strait of Hormuz triggered ballistic missile retaliation as Brent crude climbed above $90 a barrel Monday.
story: Miad Maleki, senior fellow at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, tells Fox News Digital that mounting economic pressure could push Iran to escalate in an effort to force Washington back to the negotiating table. Photos credit: Reuters/Getty

President Donald Trump declared Iran a "Failed Nation" Monday, claiming the country is economically and militarily broken as renewed fighting with the U.S. raises questions about how much leverage Tehran still has left.

"Iran is officially a Failed Nation. IT IS DEAD!" Trump wrote on Truth Social Monday morning. "They have no Navy, they have no Air Force, they have no currency, they are not paying their soldiers or police."
Trump also claimed Iranian inflation had reached 300% and said the country's leadership was "in total disarray and incapable of properly representing the country."

Iran is facing pressure from nearly every direction — renewed U.S. military strikes, tighter sanctions and a steep drop in oil exports — raising fresh questions about how long Tehran can keep absorbing the economic pain and still maintain leverage against Washington.
COULD IRAN’S REGIME COLLAPSE? EXPERTS ASSESS BESSENT’S BID TO SEVER FINANCIAL LIFELINES
Ships are anchored in the Strait of Hormuz on August 10, 2026, off the coast of Bandar Abbas, Iran. (Ali Saeedi/Getty Images)
Official Iranian data cited by Reuters put annual inflation at 66% in July, while the IMF projects average consumer-price inflation of 68.9% in 2026.

Trump's post came amid the sharpest U.S.-Iran military escalation in weeks. U.S. forces struck two Iranian launchers on Larak Island Sunday after Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps forces were observed preparing to launch rockets with sea mines into the Strait of Hormuz, according to a U.S. official. Iran retaliated by launching ballistic missiles toward U.S. bases in Jordan, while Jordan said it intercepted eight missiles that entered its airspace.
The renewed confrontation comes as Washington ratchets up economic pressure.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Reuters Sunday that the administration expects to roll out additional secondary sanctions as frequently as every week, initially focusing on banks and potentially cutting financial institutions that continue facilitating Iranian transactions out of the U.S. dollar-based financial system.
IRAN’S DEEPEST WEAKNESS IS GETTING EXPOSED THROUGH AMERICA’S MAXIMUM PRESSURE CAMPAIGN

An Iranian navy special forces service member, known as Takavaran, stands guard near the Iranian Kharg replenishment ship docked in the Red Sea Sudanese town of Port Sudan on Oct. 31, 2012. The visit of two Iranian naval ships to Sudan reflects strong ties between the countries, Sudan's military said after Khartoum denied Iranian involvement in weapons manufacturing. (Ashraf Shazly/AFP via Getty Images)
Iran's own leaders are acknowledging growing economic strain.

President Masoud Pezeshkian said Iran's exports and imports have fallen nearly 35% because of U.S. sanctions and the naval blockade, while annual inflation reached 66% in July, Reuters reported Aug. 29. The IMF projects Iran's economy will contract 5.4% this year.

Miad Maleki, a senior fellow at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies who previously served as associate director of Treasury's Office of Global Targeting at the Office of Foreign Assets Control, told Fox News Digital that the Islamic Republic may be nearing an economic breaking point. FDD says Maleki previously helped oversee U.S. sanctions programs and served as chief and senior sanctions coordinator for Iran and the Middle East.

"I think where we stand today, it's very clear — we see very clear signs, indications of what I would call an economy that is on the verge of collapse, if it hasn't already collapsed yet," Maleki said.
Maleki argued that the critical pressure point is Iran's ability to turn oil exports into usable revenue.
US TARGETS CHINESE REFINERY IN SWEEPING IRAN OIL CRACKDOWN, SANCTIONS ‘SHADOW FLEET’ TANKERS
Oil tankers and cargo ships line up in the Strait of Hormuz as seen from Khor Fakkan, United Arab Emirates, Wednesday, March 11, 2026. (Altaf Qadri/AP Photo)

He estimates Tehran needs roughly 1 million barrels of oil exports per day to sustain itself, about 1.5 million to avoid hyperinflation and approximately 2 million to support development. Maleki said Iranian exports have fallen dramatically and Tehran is increasingly struggling to repatriate revenue from the oil it can sell.
Kpler data cited by Reuters showed Chinese imports of Iranian crude falling from an average 1.4 million barrels per day in 2025 to a provisional 534,000 barrels per day so far in August.
Maleki said Tehran is increasingly relying on money creation rather than cutting politically sensitive salaries and pensions. But there are limits.
"They can keep printing money, but they can't really print the type of commodities that they need, such as gasoline, such as wheat," he said.
The pressure, however, may create a dangerous paradox.
IRAN COULD UNLEASH ‘KINETIC’ RESPONSE AS US TIGHTENS ECONOMIC CONTAINMENT, ANALYST WARNS
An Iranian woman shops in a local market in Tehran, Iran, April 28, 2026. (Majid Asgaripour/WANA (West Asia News Agency) via Reuters)

Iran analyst Danny Citrinowicz, a fellow at Israel's Institute for National Security Studies and a nonresident senior fellow at the Atlantic Council's Scowcroft Middle East Security Initiative, told Fox News Digital that the maritime blockade, wartime losses and wider economic pressure are hurting Tehran, but argued Washington should not assume economic pain will lead to capitulation.

Citrinowicz said continued pressure could instead increase Tehran's incentive to escalate if Iranian leaders conclude the status quo is worse than renewed confrontation. He said Iran could attempt to target "U.S. economic assets in the Gulf," ports or U.S. vessels involved in enforcing the blockade, even as its missile-production capabilities have been degraded.
Maleki agreed Iran would likely attempt to escalate, but questioned how much leverage Tehran still possesses.

"They're going to try to escalate," Maleki said, pointing to the attacks of the last 24 hours. But he argued that further escalation would increasingly affect Gulf states Iran has relied upon for trade, sanctions evasion and diplomacy — potentially bringing even greater economic and diplomatic pressure.
MILLIONS OF BARRELS OF IRANIAN OIL SIT BEYOND TRUMP BLOCKADE AS HE VOWS ‘ZERO LEAKAGE’
People shop for produce at the historic Tajrish bazaar in northern Tehran on Aug. 25, 2026. (AFP via Getty Images)
Asked whether Iran was losing its leverage, Maleki responded: "Absolutely."
He argued Tehran has emerged weakened from internal unrest and the external war and is increasingly isolated domestically and internationally.
What Maleki is watching next is not necessarily missed government payrolls, but shortages that could trigger another wave of domestic unrest.

"What I'm looking for is shortages of items such as gasoline," Maleki said. "Right now they're fighting a war inside Iran that is way more challenging to the regime than it is from external forces that they're facing."

Commercial traffic through the Strait of Hormuz remained severely disrupted Monday, while Brent crude climbed more than 2% to above $90 as markets reacted to the renewed U.S.-Iran exchanges. Reuters reported Aug. 31 that Gulf oil flows have recovered from their wartime lows but remain below pre-war levels.
Maleki said he expects Iranians to return to the streets and argued Western governments should prepare now to help them communicate and organize if Tehran again shuts down internet access.

"What we need to do is to contain this regime, cut off this economic lifeline, empower the Iranian people, be prepared next time Iranians are back on the street [and] take actions to stop this regime from slaughtering Iranians," Maleki said.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The Iranian internet blackout started Jan.8 and cost $1.56 million per hour amid protests. (Maria / Middle East Images / AFP via Getty Images)

"Those are the right policies — put the pressure on, be prepared to push back on the Iranian regime every time it escalates," he added. "At this point, they are the weakest they've been since 1979. Every time they try to escalate, they become weaker."
Reuters contributed to this story.

Lachter’s reporting has taken her into conflict zones and crisis areas across the Middle East, Europe, Asia and Africa. Her work has included uncovering human trafficking networks, revealing an ISIS underground torture prison in Syria, documenting the war in Ukraine and interviewing senior political figures and world leaders. She also won two Rockower Awards for Excellence in Reporting. She holds a bachelor's degree in communication and a master's degree in political science.

title: Roughly 80 Americans still unaccounted for after Himalayan disaster kills 903, officials say
summary: Nepal and China's death toll climbed to 903 as roughly 4,200 people remained unaccounted for following the devastating flood and debris flow.
story: Isha Foundation coordination leader Jyoti Jankowski discusses efforts to locate the missing people in the deadly Nepal-Tibet floods on 'Fox & Friends Weekend.'
Roughly 80 Americans remain unaccounted for following the catastrophic Himalayan flood last Wednesday that killed hundreds of people, the State Department said.
The update marks a decrease from a previous estimate of at least 90 Americans who went missing near the Nepal-China border.
"We can confirm that 13 American citizens have made their way to safety in Nepal," a State Department spokesperson told Fox News.
Meanwhile, Nepal’s death toll has risen to 903, while the number of people still unaccounted for has nearly doubled to roughly 4,200, according to an update from local officials Sunday.
TRAPPED NEPALI WORKERS PULLED FROM HYDROPOWER TUNNEL AFTER CATASTROPHIC FLOODING
A drone view shows mud covering properties following a flash flood at Trishuli in Nuwakot district, Nepal, August 26, 2026. (REUTERS/Stringer)

According to officials, the disaster occurred in north-central Nepal when a distant slope failure involving a glacier triggered a rapidly moving debris flow that traveled roughly 62 miles downstream before striking a populated area. Footage from the disaster showed a massive surge of water and debris suddenly rushing through the valleys, engulfing buildings in its path.
On Sunday, a spokesperson for Nepal’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs provided an update on the toll.

"So far, 903 bodies have been recovered from the areas and about 4200 people are still unaccounted for. Over 10,000 people have been rescued from the regions, including over 323 foreign nationals. As per the available data, about 590 foreign nationals are still missing, from 39 countries," the spokesperson said.

Twenty-two of the missing Americans were part of a pilgrimage affiliated with a Tennessee-based nonprofit group, Isha Foundation coordination leader Jyoti Jankowski told Fox News Saturday. They were inside an immigration building when the flooding struck the area, Jankowski said.
MORE THAN 3,000 MISSING AFTER COLOMBIA EARTHQUAKE AS TRUMP ADMINISTRATION PROVIDES $15.5 MILLION IN RELIEF

A drone view shows a man walking next to damaged buildings and houses covered in mud near the Likhu River following deadly flash floods and mudslides in Devighat, Nuwakot district, Nepal, on Aug. 30, 2026. (REUTERS)
Authorities said Nepal is coordinating with neighboring countries and the international community to provide relief, with supplies already arriving from countries including India and China.

More supplies are expected to arrive from the U.S., United Arab Emirates, Myanmar, Qatar, the U.K., Australia, the Republic of Korea, Japan, New Zealand, Malaysia, Singapore, Bangladesh, Pakistan and other international organizations, officials said.

"Relief and humanitarian assistance are being provided in the affected areas. We are deeply grateful to our friends and partners for their solidarity, goodwill and generous offers of support at this difficult time," the spokesperson said.
DEATH TOLL FROM MUDSLIDES, FLOODING AT NEPAL-CHINA BORDER CLIMBS PAST 670; NEARLY 3,000 MISSING
Employees retrieve banknotes near a bank covered in sludge after flash floods in Trishuli in Nepal's Nuwakot district on Aug. 30, 2026. (AFP via Getty Images)
The State Department said last Wednesday that it was "monitoring the situation and is deploying a disaster response advisor to the region to support response efforts."

"The Department will also provide $500,000 in assistance through its global award with Catholic Relief Services, supporting emergency shelter, relief items, and water, sanitation, and hygiene assistance to flood-affected communities," the department said.

According to the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) investigators remain uncertain whether the initial failure was a landslide incorporating part of a glacier or a glacial collapse, in which a portion of a glacier breaks off and rapidly moves downslope with surrounding debris.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The glacier-related event resulted in a magnitude 5.2 earthquake, according to the USGS. A second seismic event was recorded approximately three hours later, generating energy equivalent to a magnitude 4.2 earthquake.

"The glacial debris contained water and ice that rapidly melted, picking up more material and water as it flowed downslope in the existing stream and river channels, creating a fast-moving, far-traveled landslide and flood laden with boulders and other rubble," the agency said.
Bonny Chu is a Breaking and Trending News Writer for Fox News Digital

title: New report exposes intact Iranian bunker that may hide regime's ongoing nuclear work
summary: The bunkered Natanz structure was built between 2010 and 2017, raising urgent questions about Iran's uranium enrichment capabilities after two wars.
story: President Trump warns that Iran would "absolutely" use a nuclear weapon if obtained. Retired Gen. Jack Keane joins Brian Kilmeade to analyze U.S. economic sanctions and military deterrence in the Middle East.
A new report from a leading think tank has revealed what it says is a partially submerged Iranian uranium facility at the Natanz nuclear compound in Iran.

The revelation of the secretive facility raises new concerns over whether Iran’s nuclear weapons apparatus was destroyed during the two American-Israeli-launched wars against the regime in 2025 and 2026.

The Washington, D.C.-based Institute for Science and International Security (ISIS) announced in late August that it has located an underground Iranian facility that is likely linked to uranium enrichment for the possible use in production of atomic weapons.
EXPERTS ‘DEEPLY’ CONCERNED OVER IRAN’S WORK AT UNDERGROUND NUCLEAR SITE
An illustration showing a list of Iran's nuclear facilities, such as Arak's heavy water nuclear reactor and the Natanz enrichment plant.   (FDD/Fox News)

It wrote that "The facility does not appear to have been targeted in the military actions of either 2025 or 2026. Since the June 2025 war, no vehicle activity has been observed at the facility in available satellite imagery."

According to the institute, "The Institute has identified a separately enclosed, partially below-ground, bunkered building at the Natanz Nuclear Complex that was likely intended to serve as uranium hexafluoride… storage facility to support large-scale uranium enrichment at the Natanz Fuel Enrichment Plant. The bunkered structure was constructed between 2010 and 2017, with the bulk of construction occurring between 2015 and 2017."

It further added that "The lesson for today is that any temporary enrichment ban must include a dismantlement and dissolution of remaining capabilities and must not allow for any type of preparatory activity for the end of a ban."
IRAN NUCLEAR DEAL HINGES ON IAEA ACCESS TO LONG-BLOCKED ATOMIC WEAPON SITES, EXPERTS SAY

FILE - This photo released on Nov. 5, 2019, by the Atomic Energy Organization of Iran shows centrifuge machines in the Natanz uranium enrichment facility in central Iran.  (Atomic Energy Organization of Iran via AP, File)

Uranium is the crucial material to produce atomic weapons. Iran’s regime is vehemently opposed to the Trump administration’s demands that it stop enriching uranium and hand over its already enriched uranium.

According to another report by the Institute for Science and International Security in April," From December 2024 to June 2025, a half-year period, Iran almost doubled its stock of 60% enriched uranium to 440 kilograms. This action dramatically increased suspicion that Iran was moving toward a decision to build nuclear weapons, significantly shortening timelines to be able to create a nuclear arsenal with up to ten nuclear weapons."
The U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran’s vast nuclear weapons facility during Operation Midnight Hammer in June 2025 significantly set back Iran’s ability to produce atomic weapons and enrich uranium.
OBAMA-ERA INSPECTION FLAWS IN IRAN COULD PERSIST AS EXPERTS WARN OF NUCLEAR BLIND SPOTS
Iran's President, Masoud Pezeshkian, said they would rebuild the nuclear facilities targeted by the U.S., and make them stronger in 2025. (Iranian Presidency / Handout/Anadolu via Getty Images)

Jason Brodsky, policy director at United Against Nuclear Iran (UANI), told Fox News Digital that "The report assesses the structure at the Natanz nuclear facility was not targeted during Operations Midnight Hammer and Epic Fury. This raises questions as to why the U.S. and Israel did not target the site. Given that Iran is not allowing IAEA [International Atomic Energy Agency] inspections of bombed facilities, in contravention of its NPT [Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons]obligations, this will require Washington and Jerusalem to rely on their own intelligence estimates as to this bunkered building."

Brodsky added, "If it is still intact and can accommodate this kind of enrichment activity, the site should be destroyed in any future strikes. The allowance of such a facility under the JCPOA [Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action] demonstrates the flaws of the agreement — permitting Iran to retain an industrial scale enrichment program following the sunsets of various provisions — and underscores why zero enrichment in Iran has to continue to be the international demand."

When asked about the facility and if the IAEA plans to inspect it, Fredrik Dahl, a spokesman for the IAEA, told Fox News Digital, that "The building you are referring to is well-known to the Agency as part of the Natanz site that the IAEA regularly inspected prior to mid-2025."

This photo taken on May 15, 2023, shows the logo of the International Atomic Energy Agency IAEA at the IAEA headquarters in Vienna, Austria. TO GO WITH "Interview: IAEA chief expects wider, deeper nuclear cooperation with China." (Liu Xinyu/Xinhua via Getty Images)

Asked about the report, Anna Kelly, a White House spokeswoman, told Fox News Digital that "First, Iran’s nuclear facilities were totally obliterated during Operation Midnight Hammer. Now, Operation Economic Outcast is severing every remaining economic lifeline sustaining the Islamic Republic of Iran. President Trump has been clear that Iran can never possess a nuclear weapon, and America is entering the endgame with the single greatest financial offensive ever mounted against an adversary."
Successive U.S. administrations have repeatedly designated the Islamic Republic of Iran since the 1980s as a leading state-sponsor of terrorism.

U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent’s announcement last week that the U.S. imposed the economic equivalent of the military campaign that defeated Nazi Germany on the Islamic Republic of Iran could set off a series of events leading to the dissolution of the nearly 47-year-old dictatorship in Tehran, according to experts.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Bessent’s declaration of economic warfare — formally designated Operation Economic Outcast — follows President Trump’s commitment to launch an "economic D-Day" against the clerical regime. The comprehensive U.S. economic pressure point campaign also aims to isolate the regime with respect to its efforts to rebuild its nuclear weapons facility.
Benjamin Weinthal reports on Israel, Iran, Syria, Turkey and Europe. You can follow Benjamin on Twitter @BenWeinthal, and email him at benjamin.weinthal@fox.com

title: Putin unleashes new fury on Ukraine as report exposes fear hanging over war’s end
summary: Russia launched nearly 1,500 drones in four days as Volodymyr Zelenskyy says Moscow aims to exhaust Ukraine, with daytime attacks now disrupting Kyiv.
story: Smoke rises from a warehouse near Kyiv as firefighters battle a blaze following a Russian attack on Aug. 29, according to video released by Ukraine’s State Emergency Service. (Credit: Reuters .)

Questions over whether the Russia-Ukraine war is entering a new phase are mounting as Kyiv endures repeated drone attacks and near-constant air raid alerts, including growing waves during daylight hours — an expansion beyond the nighttime barrages that have become grimly familiar to residents of the Ukrainian capital.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia launched nearly 1,500 drones over four days, more than half of them jet-powered, accusing Moscow of attempting to wear down Ukraine and its population. The attacks have repeatedly interrupted Kyiv’s metro system and daily commutes, Reuters reported Aug. 31, as residents are forced to seek shelter during daytime air raid alerts.

As Ukrainians seek some semblance of normalcy at the end of the summer and prepare for the start of the school year, the relentless attacks are again sending already exhausted Kyiv residents underground.
RUSSIA UNLEASHES NEARLY 600 MISSILES AND DRONES ON KYIV IN DEADLIEST STRIKE SINCE MAY

People react as they attend the funeral of local villages’ community head Taras Didych, who was among 38 people killed in a Russian drone strike on the village of Myla on August 28, amid Russia's attack on Ukraine, in the village of Dmytrivka, Kyiv region, Ukraine August 31, 2026. (Alina Smutko/Reuters)

Russian President Vladimir Putin has simultaneously intensified attacks on Ukraine’s warehouses and logistics network, damaging distribution centers used by major retailers and disrupting food deliveries.
Russian drone attacks on Kyiv and the surrounding region stretched into a fifth consecutive day Monday, with strikes damaging warehouses, a retail outlet and residential buildings in the Kyiv region.

The attacks are part of a broader campaign against Ukrainian commercial and logistics infrastructure. Reuters reported Aug. 28 that Russia had targeted warehouses belonging to major supermarket chains, Ukraine’s largest private postal company and home-goods retailers.
Ukraine’s Agriculture Minister Taras Vysotskyi said that roughly 90% of the food logistics infrastructure operated by retail chains had been destroyed.
RUSSIA LAUNCHES BALLISTIC MISSILE ATTACK ON KYIV HOURS AFTER ZELENSKYY WARNS OF MAJOR STRIKE
Smoke rises in the city during a Russian drone strike, amid Russia's attack on Ukraine, in Kyiv, Ukraine August 31, 2026. (Gleb Garanich/Reuters)

"As of today, roughly speaking, 90% of food logistics operated by retail chains have been destroyed, but that doesn't mean Ukrainians will be left without food," Vysotskyi told reporters in Kyiv, according to Ukrainian state news agency Ukrinform. He said retailers would shift logistics and use alternative methods of delivering food.

Ukrainian outlet TSN reported Aug. 30 that some NOVUS locations in Kyiv were short of bread, potatoes, apples and oatmeal, while supermarket chain ATB had introduced limits on how much of certain products customers could purchase.

Ukraine, meanwhile, has expanded its own campaign against Russian economic infrastructure. Ukrainian drones have targeted oil facilities as well as warehouses connected to major Russian online retailers, including Wildberries and Ozon. Reuters reported Monday that a logistics hub in Yekaterinburg was also struck by a drone.

Retired Air Force Lt. Gen. Richard Newton, a former USAF assistant vice chief of staff, told Fox News Digital that he believes the military momentum has increasingly shifted toward Ukraine, particularly because of Kyiv’s expanding use of long-range drones.
ZELENSKYY SAYS PUTIN 'LOST THE INITIATIVE' AS UKRAINE'S TECH INDUSTRY RESHAPES THE WAR
Empty shelves in supermarkets in Kyiv, August 31st, 2026. (East2west news)

"My sense is the momentum has swung in Ukraine's favor over the last year or so," Newton told Fox News Digital. "The Ukrainians have shown tremendous resolve and capability to push back against Russia."

Newton pointed particularly to Ukrainian strikes deep inside Russia against "energy production capability, logistics supply chains, and so forth," calling their use of drone warfare "quite remarkable."
He cautioned, however, that Ukraine faces a critical vulnerability as Russia intensifies its aerial campaign.
"The current challenge facing Ukraine is the shortage of U.S.-made Patriot air defense interceptors," Newton said, noting that the systems are also in heavy demand elsewhere around the world.
TRUMP SAYS US WILL LET UKRAINE MAKE PATRIOT MISSILES IN MAJOR POLICY SHIFT

Emergency workers use heavy equipment to clear rubble from apartment buildings in Lviv, the westernmost city in Ukraine and the closest to NATO-ally Poland, after a Russian missile attack Thursday, July 30, 2026. (Anadolu)
The escalation comes amid new reporting about Putin’s calculations over how — or whether — the war can end.

The Economist reported Aug. 30, that Putin fears ending the war without Russia achieving even what he considers a minimum objective — control of all of Donbas — could threaten his position and potentially his physical safety.

"They will hang me," Putin reportedly told people around him at some point during the war, according to an unnamed insider cited by The Economist. Fox News Digital has not independently verified Putin remarks.

The Economist also reported that dissatisfaction with the war is growing among ordinary Russians and that the mood among parts of Russia’s elite is even more pessimistic, with one source arguing that nearly five years consumed by the war represents a failure regardless of its eventual outcome.
Newton argued that the intensifying confrontation makes NATO cohesion increasingly important.

Russian glide bombs strike a food processing plant in Zaporizhzhia. Rescuers work at the site of a reported strike on a food processing plant in Zaporizhzhia, Ukraine, on July 8, 2026. The incident involves guided aerial bombs, resulting in the destruction of part of the facility. A 43-year-old employee is injured, and several vehicles are damaged. (Dmytro Smolienko/Ukrinform/NurPhoto via Getty Images)

"In my view it's more important now for NATO to remain firm perhaps at any time since the end of the Cold War," he said. "A weakened NATO emboldens Putin and Russia not only against Ukraine but the entire alliance."

She was also among the Western journalists who entered Russia after the war began to bring testimonies from Putin’s opposition. title: U.S. strikes 3 Iranian oil tankers after Iran targets Navy warships, military says
summary: U.S. forces struck three Iranian oil tankers Saturday after Iran launched ballistic missiles toward two U.S.
story: U.S. forces struck three Iranian oil tankers Saturday after Iran launched ballistic missiles toward two U.S. Navy ships, the U.S. military said.
A U.S. aircraft carrier and guided missile destroyer evaded multiple attacks by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, U.S. Central Command said in a statement. No American personnel were harmed.

CENTCOM said U.S. forces retaliated by permanently disabling two crude oil carriers, the M/T Downy off the coast of Kharg Island and the M/T Stark 1 near Jask. Forces also destroyed a third vessel, the M/T Kylo near the Gulf of Oman.
The Kylo was not carrying oil at the time and its crew was directed to abandon the vessel before American forces struck it in multiple locations, CENTCOM said.

“If you shoot at two of our ships, we will impose an even higher economic cost — taking out three of yours,” Adm. Brad Cooper, the commander of CENTCOM, said in a statement. “We will not hesitate to defend American forces, and if necessary, destroy Iran’s limited and exposed oil fleet.”

Kharg Island, a tiny but strategic island 15 miles off the coast of Iran in the Persian Gulf, plays a central role in the country’s oil industry. There are also military capabilities there, including air defenses and mines buried underground.

The site has repeatedly emerged as a flashpoint during the conflict. U.S. forces struck military targets on the island in March but deliberately spared its oil infrastructure. President Donald Trump said at the time that the U.S. could target the energy facilities if Iran continued interfering with shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.

The island is critical to Iran’s finances. Petras Katinas, a research fellow at the Royal United Services Institute, previously told NBC News that Kharg is the “backbone” of Iran’s oil trade infrastructure and the primary gateway for the country’s oil reserves.

Iranian media reported earlier Saturday that a tanker near Kharg had been hit by U.S. missiles and that its crew was being evacuated. No causalities were reported, according to Iran’s semiofficial Tasnim news agency.

title: Judge again blocks Trump’s effort to restrict mail voting as ballots start going out
summary: The move comes as the Trump administration is appealing a related order to the Supreme Court.
story: A federal judge on Friday temporarily blocked a bid by President Donald Trump for the U.S. Postal Service to exert control over mail-in voting ahead of the midterm elections as one state begins mailing out ballots.

Boston-based U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani, who previously blocked a related effort on mail voting, found the new Postal Service rule dictating how mail-in ballots can be sent is likely unlawful and unconstitutional, prompting her to issue a preliminary injunction.
The rushed time frame being pushed by the administration will make voter disenfranchisement “practically inevitable” if the rule is allowed to stay in place, the judge found.

The “court finds, on one side, that immediate implementation of the Final Rule issued less than seventy days before the November 2026 election threatens disenfranchisement of millions of United States citizens who seek to vote by mail,” while “on the other side, that the record includes no evidence relating to fraudulent mail voting to support the rushed implementation of the Final Rule,” Talwani wrote.
She rejected the Justice Department’s request that she pause her order while the administration appeals, and noted that her ruling does not bar states that want to follow the new rules from doing do.
Talwani also said the ruling applies only to the midterms, since “the Final Rule imposes no irreparable harm as to later elections and judicial challenges may be addressed in the normal course.”
The DOJ did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the judge’s order, but said in a court filing Friday night that it would appeal to the First Circuit Court of Appeals.
The action comes a day after the Trump administration asked the Supreme Court to override a temporary order issued by Talwani last week halting the rule.

In that ruling, the judge sided with states and voting rights groups that argued the Postal Service rule unlawfully usurped states’ power to regulate their own elections — and left them facing an “impossible” timeline to comply.

“Through the Final Rule, the USPS is refusing to send mail ballots to eligible voters unless States or local election officials submit their mail ballot envelopes and return envelopes and receive advance approval from the USPS without regard to impending deadlines for the November 3, 2026 election,” the judge wrote.

It also “requires elections officials to create accounts for a new electronic portal, certify that they have received approval regarding the mail ballot design, and thereafter upload to the USPS portal each voter’s information, including name, address, and a unique intelligent mail barcode,” she noted.

“Based on the record presently before the court, Plaintiff States face irreparable harm where they are required to comply with a likely unconstitutional regulation for which compliance is practically impossible as to the 2026 midterm elections, now little more than two months away,” Talwani wrote.

The states “have neither time nor funds to design new mail ballots, seek approval of the new designs, order production of mail ballots, update their own election management systems, train election officials to use the USPS portal, and upload citizen data to the portal, all before the midterms,” she wrote.

North Carolina began sending out ballots Friday, as required by state law. State Attorney General Jeff Jackson, a Democrat, said in a statement Thursday that if the Supreme Court sides with the administration, it would “throw our election into chaos.”
“The ballots are printed, the process is underway, and North Carolinians deserve a lawful and orderly election,” Jackson said.
In his filing to the Supreme Court, U.S. Solicitor General John Sauer argued it was Talwani and not the rush to implement the directive that’s causing “confusion.”

While her order allowed states that want to follow the new requirement to do so, that “risks sowing confusion and chaos because it makes those preparatory steps voluntary, and not mandatory,” Sauer wrote.

“Thus, if the order is eventually stayed and the rule takes effect for this year’s elections — as should occur, there is a grave risk that States may not have taken the necessary steps to comply due to the false latitude allowed by the court’s improper order, potentially depriving those States’ citizens of the ability to vote by mail,” Sauer added.
The rule change came about after an executive order issued by President Donald Trump on March 31 titled “Ensuring Citizenship Verification and Integrity in Federal Elections.”
Talwani issued an earlier order in a related case barring the rule from going into effect, but it was reversed last month by the Supreme Court, which found the rule had not yet been finalized.

“The court’s disposition of this application does not mean that any measure taken by the Government to implement the order will necessarily be lawful. On that score, time will tell,” the court said in an unsigned 6-3 ruling.
The rule was subsequently finalized late last month.
In his filing to the high court this week, Sauer argued the changes that are being implemented are “modest.”

Brooks Ghost Max 3

Labor Day sales have already started. Retailers typically consider the Friday before the official holiday, which lands on Monday, Sept. 7 this year, the start of the long weekend, so all sales are now live.

All the experts I talked to agree that the best way to save the most money during Labor Day sales is to stack your savings. That means looking at the deal price as the starting point and combining it with additional offers to save even more, says Gerstley. Since so many retailers are hosting sales right now, they’re all competing for your attention, and you never know when one might lower prices just a little bit more to give themselves an edge, or throw in extras that make a purchase more worthwhile, like free shipping, delivery, install or haul-away. Don’t be afraid to ask about price matching, too, says Carls. If a retailer really wants your business, they’ll be open to negotiating with you.

Last but not least, don’t feel like you absolutely have to buy something if deals aren’t compelling, says Gerstley. As we enter the final quarter of the year, sales are plentiful with early Black Friday and Cyber Monday offers starting in October, and Amazon Prime Big Deal Days might be around the corner (it hasn’t been confirmed yet, however). title: Man duct-taped to plane seat after hurling slurs and attacking other passenger, witness says
summary: A passenger aboard a Newark, New Jersey-bound American Airlines flight was duct-taped to his seat on Thursday and later arrested after allegedly hurling racial slurs at staff and fighting with another man. The passenger was “thrashing around” in his seat as the flight crew and other passengers tried to restrain him at the rear of the first-class cabin, according to witness Michelle Ng-Reyes.
story: A passenger aboard a Newark, New Jersey-bound American Airlines flight was duct-taped to his seat on Thursday and later arrested after allegedly hurling racial slurs at staff and fighting with another man.
The passenger was “thrashing around” in his seat as the flight crew and other passengers tried to restrain him at the rear of the first-class cabin, according to witness Michelle Ng-Reyes.

“I think he hurt himself and was bleeding on the seat and apparently was assaulting the man sitting next to him, who was another man dressed in a suit,” Ng-Reyes told NBC New York. “The three men that were holding him down were saying things like, ‘Stop moving, please stop yelling, just sit down.’”
A video obtained by TMZ shows the effort to restrain him.
Ng-Reyes, who was seated near an air marshal, said other passengers heard the man direct racially offensive remarks at the man sitting next to him.
He also appeared to target his fury at flight attendants who were Black, Ng-Reyes said.
“They had to physically restrain him ’cause they were worried he might try to go into the cockpit or something, which is obviously pretty scary,” she said.
The flight, which originated in Dallas, was diverted to Baltimore, where the passenger was removed from the plane and taken into custody, officials said. His name has not been released.

He was arrested by the Maryland Transportation Authority Police, according to a statement from the the FBI’s Baltimore field office. The agency did not respond to a request for comment on the matter and it’s unclear whether the man remains in custody.

“The FBI is currently conducting interviews to gather the facts and will consult with the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Maryland to determine if federal charges will be filed,” the statement said. A spokesperson for the U.S. attorney’s office declined to comment.
The flight was scheduled to land in Newark 3 1/2 hours after takeoff, Ng-Reyes said, but the diversion and delay stretched the trip to roughly eight hours.

“The safety ​and ​security ​of ​our customers and team members is ​our top priority ​and ​we do ​not ​tolerate violence,” American Airlines said in a statement. “We thank ​our team members ​for their ​professionalism and our customers ​for their understanding.”

title: Dolly Parton’s sister slams ‘fake AI garbage’ flooding the internet since icon’s death
summary: Dolly Parton’s sister has condemned the AI deepfakes circulating in the wake of the beloved American icon’s death.
story: Dolly Parton’s sister has condemned the AI deepfakes circulating in the wake of the beloved American icon’s death.
Stella Parton, 77, addressed the fake AI-generated images and videos being of her sister in a statement shared to Instagram Friday, where she also thanked fans for their “genuine” support.

“Sadly, because of the way our lives have been lived in front of the public, we have no choice but to be subjected to incredible pressure and insensitivity from strangers,” she wrote. “There is a tremendous amount of AI and endless garbage being posted everyday and it’s been challenging to absorb and or ignore.”
“As time passes, those who are in the business of exploiting the loss and tragedies of others on a daily basis will move on to the next stampede of endless misinformation,” she added.
It marks Stella’s most extensive comments yet on the online reaction since the larger-than-life country singer died a little more than a week ago following a brief battle with cancer. She was 80.

The younger Parton is a country singer and songwriter in her own right. Stella had several hit songs in the 1970s, including “I Want to Hold You in My Dreams Tonight,” which was released in 1975. She is one of the American icon’s 11 siblings.
“We will be okay in time but each of us will grieve in our own personal way,” she wrote. “Every human being experiences pain and loss in life and my family is no different.”
Stella Parton said that her “big sister Dolly would be surprised and delighted by the love her family and she has been shown during this time.”
“She loved her fans and the public in general,” she wrote. “That is the reason she chose not to express her opinions on a lot of things like politics, religion and individuals in the public eye.”
She asked fans to “show more compassion and wisdom as we move forward in life.”
“Use my sister’s life as an example for tolerance and respect toward others,” she wrote. “It’s not about the most clever comments, fake AI garbage or snarky tweets.”
“At the end of the day or the end of a life, how will you feel about yourself?”

title: U.S. strikes 3 Iranian oil tankers after Iran targets Navy warships, military says
summary: U.S. forces struck three Iranian oil tankers Saturday after Iran launched ballistic missiles toward two U.S.
story: U.S. forces struck three Iranian oil tankers Saturday after Iran launched ballistic missiles toward two U.S. Navy ships, the U.S. military said.
A U.S. aircraft carrier and guided missile destroyer evaded multiple attacks by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, U.S. Central Command said in a statement. No American personnel were harmed.

CENTCOM said U.S. forces retaliated by permanently disabling two crude oil carriers, the M/T Downy off the coast of Kharg Island and the M/T Stark 1 near Jask. Forces also destroyed a third vessel, the M/T Kylo near the Gulf of Oman.
The Kylo was not carrying oil at the time and its crew was directed to abandon the vessel before American forces struck it in multiple locations, CENTCOM said.

“If you shoot at two of our ships, we will impose an even higher economic cost — taking out three of yours,” Adm. Brad Cooper, the commander of CENTCOM, said in a statement. “We will not hesitate to defend American forces, and if necessary, destroy Iran’s limited and exposed oil fleet.”

Kharg Island, a tiny but strategic island 15 miles off the coast of Iran in the Persian Gulf, plays a central role in the country’s oil industry. There are also military capabilities there, including air defenses and mines buried underground.

The site has repeatedly emerged as a flashpoint during the conflict. U.S. forces struck military targets on the island in March but deliberately spared its oil infrastructure. President Donald Trump said at the time that the U.S. could target the energy facilities if Iran continued interfering with shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.

The island is critical to Iran’s finances. Petras Katinas, a research fellow at the Royal United Services Institute, previously told NBC News that Kharg is the “backbone” of Iran’s oil trade infrastructure and the primary gateway for the country’s oil reserves.

Iranian media reported earlier Saturday that a tanker near Kharg had been hit by U.S. missiles and that its crew was being evacuated. No causalities were reported, according to Iran’s semiofficial Tasnim news agency.

title: Illinois mother charged with murder in death of her 2-year-old
summary: A suburban Illinois mother who had become interested in the Lindsay Clancy case has been charged with murder after she allegedly killed her 2-year-old son then attempted to harm herself, according to police and court records.
story: A suburban Illinois mother who had become interested in the Lindsay Clancy case has been charged with murder after she allegedly killed her 2-year-old son then attempted to harm herself, according to police and court records.

A quiet street in the affluent village of Frankfort, Illinois, about 35 miles southwest of Chicago, became a scene of terror earlier this week when the 2-year-old child was found hanging in the basement and his mother, Corie A. Walsh, was discovered in a bathtub in an apparent suicide attempt.
Walsh, 40, was charged with three counts of first-degree murder on Friday, police announced.
Before the killing, Walsh had “recently become very invested in the Lindsay Clancy murder trial,” prosecutors said in their petition to deny her pretrial release.
Clancy, who killed her three children in January 2023, has been in the national spotlight amid her livestreamed murder trial. It culminated in a mistrial Friday.

Walsh had been “actively discussing the case” in group text messages with her friends up until 12:30 p.m. Tuesday — just three and a half hours before the grisly scene at her home was discovered, the filing said. At the time, the Clancy jury was in deliberations.
Frankfort police responded to the home just after 4 p.m. Tuesday on a report of an unresponsive child, authorities said.
When officers arrived, they found a neighbor performing CPR on the toddler, Barrett Walsh, whom she had found hanging in the basement, court documents said.
The neighbor took the child down and attempted CPR while calling 911, but he was already cold with no pulse, prosecutors said.

The child was transported to a local hospital, where he was pronounced dead. The Will County Coroner’s Office ruled his death an apparent homicide. Preliminary findings of the autopsy say he died from asphyxia due to ligature compression of the neck, the petition said.

Officers found Walsh in the bathroom of the upstairs master bedroom, lying in a tub fully dressed and “surrounded by bloody water.” Walsh was found with cuts to her wrists and thighs, the petition said. She was taken to a hospital with non-life-threatening injuries, police said.
Walsh told officers “she did this to her baby because he was the ‘devil’ and the ‘anti-Christ,’” the filing said.

The neighbor told officers she had found Walsh with a knife in her hands, “actively harming herself.” The neighbor took the knife and threw it into the sink, and it was later taken into evidence, according to the petition.
After she took the knife away, Walsh asked her why she did that, “as she was trying to kill herself,” the petition said.
Walsh then told the neighbor that “Bear,” the child’s nickname, was “in the basement,” the filing said.
Police said Wednesday that the preliminary investigation indicated it was a domestic-related homicide.
Walsh’s husband was out of town at the time. An infant was home  and unharmed, prosecutors said.
Two school-age children had returned home around the time Barrett was found and they were also physically unharmed, the filing said.
Walsh allegedly made statements regarding harming her other children and harming her husband upon his return home, prosecutors said in the filing.
Once hospitalized, she also described to officers “the manner in which she killed Barrett,” which was consistent with evidence at the scene, the petition said.
Walsh was in custody Friday night and being held for medical treatment. Once released, she’ll be transferred to the Will County Adult Detention Facility.
It was not immediately clear whether she has retained an attorney.
Frankfort police called the case a “heartbreaking tragedy,” saying, “We ask our community to keep them in their thoughts and prayers.”

title: Burning Man attendee dies at festival after medical emergency
summary: A man died while attending the annual Burning Man festival in the Nevada desert this week, the festival said Thursday.
story: A man died while attending the annual Burning Man festival in the Nevada desert this week, the festival said Thursday.
The festivalgoer was described as being in his mid-50s and had a medical emergency at the event, it said in a statement.
He “immediately received lifesaving measures, and was transported to the onsite center for emergency care where he was pronounced deceased,” the festival said.

The man’s identity was being withheld until family could be notified, it said. The Pershing County Sheriff’s Office, which doubles as the region’s medical examiner, did not immediately respond to a request for information.
The cause and manner of death have not been released.
“The safety and well-being of our community and staff remain our highest priority,” the festival said.
The death came as the festival endured another year with weather woes, including rain on Friday that temporarily closed a main gate to festival grounds known as Black Rock City.

By 6 p.m. on Friday the gate was reopened, organizers said in a discussion board post. The National Weather Service called for blowing dust early Friday evening and a 20% chance of rain on Sunday for nearby Gerlach, Nevada, a community of 58 people about 100 miles north of Reno.

The festival, with a capacity of 80,000 people, also was hit with mud and rain in 2023 as many attendees were trapped on its grounds, where vehicle traffic was temporarily limited and some hiked in the mud to nearby towns.
Burning Man kicked off Aug. 30 and is scheduled through Sept. 7.

The post-hippie, psychedelic festival of DJ-performed music, art installations, and temporary communal living takes place each year on 3,400 acres of dry lake and desert land in northern Nevada run by the U.S. Bureau of Land Management.

It’s celebrating its 40th year, with its roots in a 1986 gathering on San Francisco’s Baker Beach said to have drawn roughly 20 people for the planned, bonfire burning of an 8-foot wooden structure known as “the Man.”

title: Judge orders Trump officials to disclose who set up the $1.8B ‘anti-weaponization’ fund
summary: The ruling comes in a lawsuit first filed by a fired Jan. 6 prosecutor and a law professor seeking to block the “anti-weaponization” fund.
story: A federal judge on Friday ordered the Trump administration to identify the people who came up with the structure for the nearly $1.8 billion “anti-weaponization fund” that Attorney General Todd Blanche has said is now “dead.”

U.S. Magistrate Judge Ivan D. Davis of the Eastern District of Virginia issued an order that granted part of a motion from plaintiffs to compel discovery from the federal government, a person who was in the courtroom when the order was issued confirmed to NBC News. The order includes disclosing the names of the fund’s architects, the person said.
The New York Times reported on the details of the judge’s order.

“Today’s order granting discovery is a significant step in getting to the bottom of the slush fund,” Aman George, senior counsel at Democracy Forward, a nonprofit organization representing the plaintiffs, said in a statement. “We will continue to meet the government in court until our investigation is complete and the slush fund is permanently halted.”
The Justice Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment Friday evening.

The fund — established as part of a settlement agreement between President Donald Trump, two of his sons and his company, and the Internal Revenue Service — aimed to set aside roughly $1.8 billion in taxpayer money as payouts for those who “suffered weaponization and lawfare” — a provision that could extend to Jan. 6 rioters convicted, and later pardoned by Trump, for violent crimes.

It was temporarily blocked in May by a federal judge following a lawsuit filed by a fired Jan. 6 prosecutor and a law professor who had been sued by the Trump administration. Career IRS workers also joined the lawsuit against the Trump-IRS agreement, which made the president and several family members immune from IRS audits.
Add to Google
Add to Google

The “anti-weaponization” fund drew bipartisan criticism in Washington, putting Blanche’s nomination as attorney general in jeopardy. He later put in writing that the fund “is rescinded” and that “there is no fund.” But in a major legal loophole, the document signed by Blanche did not include the signatories of the initial agreement, meaning the fund and related IRS immunity could be revived at a later date.

That loophole has lingered as Trump has refused to denounce the fund. At a Cabinet meeting this summer, Trump, who has not ruled out giving payouts to Jan. 6 rioters, said that the fund “is dead, but you know, I wish it weren’t,” and reiterated that he thinks “people were horribly treated.”

This week, Treniss Evans III, a Jan. 6 defendant who is seeking a $1 million payout from the government, posted a photo of himself in Blanche’s office, though a person familiar with the matter said that Evans did not meet with the attorney general. Evans was previously sentenced to 20 days in prison and three years probation due to his participation in storming the Capitol.

title: Texas AG Paxton investigates military healthcare contractor over denied claims
summary: Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton has opened an investigation into a major military healthcare contractor over wrongfully denied medical claims.
story: Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton has opened an investigation into a major military healthcare contractor over wrongfully denied medical claims.

Paxton’s office said in a release this week that complaints have surged against TriWest Healthcare Alliance because the company is denying claims due to errors that incorrectly listed some beneficiaries as having “Other Health Insurance,” or OHI.

“Health insurance companies cannot promise health care coverage and then wrongfully deny patients the benefits they are entitled to receive,” Paxton said in the release. The investigation will examine whether TriWest’s handling of the claims violated Texas consumer protection law.
TriWest is one of the contractors that administers TRICARE, the military’s healthcare program for active-duty service members, retirees and their families.

In May, NBC News reported on persistent problems beneficiaries have faced since 2025, when TRICARE transitioned its contract from Health Net Federal Services to TriWest. The reporting included the case of Guy Shoemaker, 65, of Fort Worth Texas, who said he had tens of thousands of dollars in previously approved claims overturned and money clawed back from paid providers because of an OHI error.

Shoemaker, a retired Army sergeant first class and recruiter who spent a year in Afghanistan, was diagnosed with Stage 2 throat cancer in 2021 and has since needed ongoing therapy to ensure he can speak and swallow safely. The lull in coverage led to serious deterioration of his condition. Another 13 beneficiaries also spoke to NBC News, describing problems with their TRICARE coverage following the transition to TriWest.
Paxton, who is currently running for Senate as a Republican against Democrat James Talarico,  mentioned Shoemaker in his press release.

“Mr. Shoemaker tried to correct the issue with TriWest for almost two years. He only received relief after NBC aired a news story covering his situation,” the press release said. “The Shoemakers’ situation is not unique and TriWest has acknowledged the OHI denials are [a] problem.”
Shortly after NBC News’ story on Shoemaker aired, TriWest President and CEO David McIntyre Jr. apologized to those who had experienced problems with OHI errors under the company’s watch.
“I want to personally take this opportunity to apologize to those of you who have experienced challenges with Other Health Insurance on our watch,” McIntyre wrote in a letter to beneficiaries in May.
In an emailed statement Friday, TriWest said the company is reviewing Paxton’s investigative demand.
“We and the 146,000 providers in our Texas network are committed to military families, helping ensure they receive the care they have earned,” the statement said.

In an interview Friday, Shoemaker, who is now covered by Medicare, said the Texas investigation is “nice to see,” but believes the issue should be addressed nationally. For him, however, “the damage is done” — even though his coverage problems were resolved, his condition is “going to progressively get worse,” Shoemaker said.
“I know the issue still exists for other veterans,” Shoemaker said. “I’ll give Ken Paxton credit. I appreciate the fact that he’s taking it up, but again, it should be more than just state level.”

Paxton’s office said it had issued civil investigative demands to TriWest seeking information from the company and plans to interview consumers and employees. The investigation will determine whether TriWest violated the Texas Deceptive Trade Practices Act.

title: Dolly Parton’s Sister Slams ‘AI And Endless Garbage’ Amid Grief: ‘Show More Compassion’
summary: Dolly Parton’s sister Stella Parton has spoken out against some of the recent AI social media posts that have followed the country icon’s death.
story: Dolly Parton’s sister has spoken out against some of the recent social media posts that have followed the country icon’s passing, which she says have been difficult to tolerate.

Stella Parton, 77, slammed the “tremendous amount of AI and endless garbage” on social media in the wake of the death of her sister Dolly Parton. The “Jolene” singer died Aug. 25 after a brief battle with cancer, her estate said in a statement.

“Sadly, because of the way our lives have been lived in front of the public, we have no choice but to be subjected to incredible pressure and insensitivity from strangers,” Stella Parton, a country singer and songwriter herself, wrote in an Sept. 4 Instagram post. “There is a tremendous amount of AI and endless garbage being posted everyday and it’s been challenging to absorb and or ignore.”
Stella Parton condemned “those who are in the business of exploiting the loss and tragedies of others,” adding that those individuals will “move on to the next stampede of endless misinformation.”

Dolly Parton died “at the Vanderbilt-Ingram Cancer Center surrounded by loved ones,” her estate said. She was preceded in death by five of her 11 siblings, who were raised in the Appalachia region of rural Tennessee by parents Robert and Avie Lee Parton, according to the Country Music Hall of Fame. Stella Parton is among her six living brothers and sisters.
In her Instagram post, Stella Parton thanked those who showed the family “‘genuine’ support and love during this time of our family bereavement.”
“We will be okay in time but each of us will grieve in our own personal way,” Stella Parton wrote. “Every human being experiences pain and loss in life and my family is no different.”
She also wrote that her sister would be “surprised and delighted” by the love that her family has been shown amid their mourning.
Stella Parton additionally praised Dolly Parton’s openness and positive influence.

“Her heart was so big and tender toward anyone who felt, as she often felt as a child,” Stella Parton wrote of her sister. “The feeling of being told you were less than, undeserving or insignificant were deep wounds on all of us as children.”
Criticizing some of the negative comments that have arisen amid the family’s journey with grief, Stella Parton called on fans to “show more compassion and wisdom as we move forward in life.”
“Use my sister’s life as an example for tolerance and respect toward others,” she wrote. “It’s not about the most clever comments, fake AI garbage or snarky tweets.”
Stella Parton added: “At the end of the day or the end of a life, how will you feel about yourself?”
“It’s not about what other individuals you will never meet think of you!” she wrote.

Stella Parton is among the family members of many late celebrities who have spoken out against the use of AI-generated images in tributes. Robin Williams’ daughter Zelda Williams also slammed the creation of deepfakes of the actor’s likeness. Robin Williams died by suicide in 2014 at age 63 while suffering from Lewy body dementia.

“If you’re just trying to troll me, I’ve seen way worse, I’ll restrict and move on. But please, if you’ve got any decency, just stop doing this to him and to me, to everyone even, full stop,” Zelda Williams previously wrote in her Instagram stories.
While Stella Parton has been vocal about some of the negativity that has followed Dolly Parton’s passing, she has also taken to social media to remember the beautiful aspects of her sister’s life.

In an Aug. 27 social media post, Stella Parton called the “Islands In the Stream” singer “one of the most generous, thoughtful and kind people I’ve ever known,” adding, “What the world saw is exactly who she was.”
“Show more kindness, lift others up and give more of your time and resources as she continued to do to the very end,” she wrote.

title: Fans Impressed by Usher Wax Figure They Say Is ‘Too Spot On’
summary: Some celebrity wax figures go viral for being unrecognizable, but Usher’s replica is capturing fans’ attention for being “too spot on.” See his reaction to the wax figure.
story: Some celebrity wax figures go viral for being unrecognizable, but Usher’s replica is capturing fans’ attention for being “too spot on.”

Madame Tussauds’ Las Vegas location unveiled its newest wax figure to Usher in a video shared on Instagram Sept. 3. Usher’s wax figure shows him posing while in the middle of hitting one of his signature dance moves.
“Wow,” the R&B singer said in the clip the instant he walked into the museum and spotted the creation.
“Look at that guy! It looks more like me than me,” he marveled as he inspected all the intricate details.
He pointed out that the artists perfectly matched his eyes.

“I’m blown away,” he added before sharing that the wax figure is sporting the same outfit he wore during his 2021 Las Vegas residency at The Colosseum at Caesars Palace. The look featured glittery red roller skates, black gloves and a “U” chain. The replica even had in-ears, the audio device musicians use when they perform.
“I hope that my fans who did not get the chance to see that show have a little bit of a glimpse of the magic that was there for my very first Vegas residency,” he shared.
In the caption, the “U Remind Me” singer quipped that now his fans know where to find him.
“I’ve officially made it back to Vegas permanently!!” he joked.
He also further complimented the Madame Tussauds creation, adding, “The details are crazy.”
Fans in the comments agreed that the wax figure was impressive, labeling it one of the best they’ve ever seen.
“Now that actually looks like the actual person. Have that person do all of them for now on even statues,” one said.
Another wrote, “I’ve never seen a wax figure look this much like the person. The person that made this has to be a fan.”
Others chimed in and poked fun at the recent rumors that Usher was using an imposter to perform for him at some stops on his joint tour with Chris Brown.
“See? The fans swore up and down you had a double. Now look!” one commented and included a crying-laughing emoji.
“You said they can’t clone you, but they sure can wax you!!!!” an Instagram user wrote. “Still doesn’t compare to the original though.”
She continued, “I guess I gotta go to Vegas to get my picture, because that’s the only way I’m getting one with you.”
But one fan playfully said she was alarmed by just how good the wax figure looked.
“This one is TOO spot on. I’m scared lol,” she said.

Usher worked personally with a team of Studio Artists from Madame Tussauds to make sure they nailed the wax figure, the museum said in a press release. The team took hundreds of measurements and photographs of the Grammy winner to include all his features.
The museum also revealed that Usher donated his residency outfit to complete the look.
“Over the course of about nine months, 20 studio artists sculpted, painted and individually inserted each piece of hair to achieve the perfect likeness,” Madame Tussauds said.

title: Tina Knowles Shares a Rare Photo Taken Moments After Beyoncé Was Born 45 Years Ago
summary: Tina Knowles shares a photo from right after Beyonce’s birth on the singer’s 45th anniversary.
story: Forty-five years ago today, a queen was born: Queen Bey.
Beyoncé is celebrating her 45th birthday on Sept. 4, 2026, and her mother, Tina Knowles, shared a glimpse into the day a star was born with a rare photo.
The photo, posted on Instagram, shows a young Knowles in a hospital bed with an even younger Beyoncé in her arms.
The photo is signed “Baby Beyoncé” with the date “9/4/1981.”

“Reminiscing on this day 45 years ago. You took nine hours to come. And I am exhausted on this photo, but the happiest I’ve ever been in my life up to this point on this day,” Knowles wrote in the caption.
She goes on to describe what’s happening in the photo.
“We are making our first eye contact. The connection is so strong and so beautiful and so powerful. It’s never been broken and it never will,” she continued.
Knowles then paid tribute to her daughter, the “extraordinary human being” that she is.
“Out of all the beautiful things about you, the thing I love the most is your huge heart! It is the thing that I’m the most proud of. You are an extraordinary human being first.”

“And even through all the sometimes terrible noise you keep going and moving forward,” Knowles said, concluding her birthday message. “Creating, loving, lifting up others constantly making history, and using that genius mind, working your butt off, minding your own damn business, and living your life to the fullest. Happy Birthday I love you ❤️🙏🏾🌹”
Knowles spoke about the meaning behind her firstborn’s name during a podcast appearance in 2021.

“A lot of people don’t know that Beyoncé is my last name. It’s my maiden name,” Knowles said on the “In My Head With Heather Thomson. “My name was Celestine Beyoncé, which at that time was not a cool thing to have that weird name. I wanted my name to be Linda Smith because those were the cool names.”

Knowles has always been very outspoken in her support for her daughter, whether it’s re-creating one of the singer’s iconic “Renaissance Tour” looks or slamming critics. She’s also a cheerleader for her second daughter, Solange.
When Beyoncé made her first Met Gala appearance in a decade and shared the spotlight with her husband Jay-Z and their daughter Blue Ivy, Knowles told TODAY she got emotional.

“It was kind of reminiscent, because Beyoncé started, you know, her first red carpet at 15, and Blue is 14,” Knowles said May 5 on the 3rd hour of TODAY. “And so just seeing her out there looking confident and beautiful, it just brought tears to my eyes.”

title: Inside Gloria Steinem’s Feminist Paradise Home, To Be Preserved as a Political Organizing Space
summary: Gloria Steinem’s New York City brownstone has been famously known as a hub for feminist organizers and activists across a swath of movements, with a history of remarkable gatherings held between its elegantly decorated walls.
story: Gloria Steinem’s New York City brownstone has been famously known as a hub for feminist organizers and activists across a swath of movements, with a history of remarkable gatherings held between its elegantly decorated walls. As activists push to preserve the iconic home after Steinem’s death this week, many are curious about what’s inside.

Nonprofit Gloria’s Foundation has said that the three-story New York City home will stand as a permanent place for political gathering and organizing. Steinem, who died on Sept. 2, passed away in the residence, “surrounded by some of the many who loved her,” according to the Instagram post on her official page.

In an installment of Architectural Digest’s “Open Door” series, Steinem gave viewers a glimpse into the storied apartment that she considered her sanctuary. And it turns out, the home was a treasure trove of historic memorabilia.

“Home means safety, shelter, friends, sleep,” she told the outlet in the 2024 house tour. “Home — I don’t want to say it’s more important than love — but it’s more permanent. And I feel that especially now, because there are so many people in the world who have no home.”

Steinem’s 1880s brownstone sits in Manhattan’s Upper East Side. Her space is an amalgamation of several apartment units in the building. And over the years, Steinem told AD, the space hosted leaders and prominent artists from Wilma Mankiller, the first woman elected Principal Chief of the Cherokee Nation, to novelist Alice Walker, the first African-American woman to win the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction.

The journalist and activist first rented the parlor floor with friend and artist Barbara Nessim in 1968, before expanding. During the house tour, Steinem showed viewers the space that she initially shared with Nessim. The two lived between two rooms and created additional sleep space by putting a bed onto a loft that they built. The loft is still there to this day.

“We built this balcony, which actually is the front porch of some unknown person in Connecticut, and was in a wrecking yard,” she recalled to AD. “So whoever got in first got the balcony, and whoever got in second got the couch in the other room.”

Steinem’s living room was the site of many iconic gatherings. That area, she showed the outlet, includes cozy plush sofas and walls covered in artwork. Among the pieces Steinem owns is a still-life painting by her mother in addition to a piece depicting Barack Obama’s inauguration.
She also pointed out a “Madonna I bought on a trip to Latin America, because she was the only Madonna of color,” she told the outlet.
While she only had a small kitchenette when she first moved in, Steinem revealed that she has since added a larger kitchen to the home — though she doesn’t necessarily use it.
“My idea of cooking is dialing,” she said, alluding to a habit of ordering takeout.

The feminist icon’s bedroom, once her shared workspace with Nessim, includes high ceilings, built-in bookcases and a library ladder. Nightstands flank Steinem’s bed. And one of the lamps, she shows in the video, is topped with tassels that have a unique story.

“Their origin was women who were working in a factory in Afghanistan, and their bosses made them cut their hair off because they thought it was a safety hazard to get their hair, you know, caught in the machinery,” Steinem said. “They meanwhile missed the whole feeling, as we can understand, of having hair that you could toss back, and so they created their own kind of headpiece with something they also could toss back.”
The guest room is just as vibrant, filled with books, artwork and its own bathroom. Steinem said that it was her way of providing lodging to movement workers when they needed it.

“I always wanted to have space for people who were visiting New York, so it allowed me to create what is often a guest room downstairs. Meanwhile, organizers, workers, political people, friends, whoever it is, need to pass through New York,” she said. “So it always seemed right to be able to contribute at least a guest room for one or two people with its own bath.”

There’s also an outdoor space, Steinem showed AD. The garden includes several highlights, such as a plaque dedicated to Mary Wollstonecraft, the 18th century English writer and philosopher whose work “A Vindication of the Rights of Woman” is largely considered a cornerstone of classic feminism.

“In my garden, I have a Mary Wollstonecraft plaque, which reminds me that various current living generations of women, who are trying to democratize a patriarchy, can identify with their courage when they had not even a separate legal identity from daughters or wives, could not vote,” Steinem said. “It’s definitely an inspiration.”
The Instagram post on Steinem’s official Instagram requests that, in lieu of sending flowers, fans can make donations to Gloria’s Foundation, which is spearheading the preservation of the home.

title: The Emmys Are in a Week. Here’s What to Absolutely Watch
summary: Here are the TV shows and performances to watch before the 2026 Emmys including The Pitt, Pluribus and Widow’s Bay.
story: “Take It From Me” is a TODAY.com series where experts use their wisdom to explain trends or make recommendations within their fields. In this latest installment, pop culture experts share their recommendations for what to watch ahead of the Emmys.
The Emmys are approaching fast, which means there are only a few more days to catch up on buzzy award shows.

The ceremony takes place on Monday, Sept. 14, on NBC. So, maybe not quite enough time to binge-watch entire series, but there’s definitely enough hours to at least get a taste of the performances that everyone will be talking about.
To narrow down what to watch, TODAY.com spoke to two pop culture experts to get their opinions:
Chris Witherspoon, founder of PopViewers and an entertainment contributor for NBC News and MSNBCKristen Maldonado, founder of the entertainment outlet Pop Culture Planet
Chris Witherspoon, founder of PopViewers and an entertainment contributor for NBC News and MSNBC
Kristen Maldonado, founder of the entertainment outlet Pop Culture Planet
Read on for their recommendations.
Front-Running Shows

Nominated for: 18 awards, including outstanding drama series; outstanding lead actress in a drama (Rhea Seehorn); outstanding supporting actor in a drama (Carlos-Manuel Vesga); and outstanding guest actress in a drama (Miriam Shor)
“Apple TV is really just nailing it lately,” Maldonado says, referring to “Pluribus” and another Emmys darling, “Widow’s Bay.”

Created by Vince Gilligan of “Breaking Bad” and “Better Call Saul,” this sci-fi series is about a woman (Rhea Seehorn) who ends up being one of the few of humanity not to be taken over by an alien virus that dissolves individuality.
“The most miserable woman on book in the world has to save everyone,” Maldonado says.

Nominated for: 19 awards, including outstanding comedy series; outstanding lead actor in a comedy (Matthew Rhys); outstanding supporting actor in a comedy (Stephen Root); and outstanding supporting actress in a comedy (Kate O’Flynn)

Created by Katie Dippold, a former “Parks and Recreation” writer, “Widow’s Bay” is set on a definitely haunted New England island, which the mayor (Matthew Rhys) is desperately trying to make palatable to tourists.
“What’s so great about ‘Widow’s Bay’ is that it’s equal parts funny and unsettling,” Maldonado says. “Katie Dippold managed to deliver something that we haven’t seen before.”

Nominated for: 25 awards, including outstanding drama series; outstanding lead actor in a drama series (Noah Wyle); outstanding supporting actress in a drama series (Sepideh Moafi, Katherine LaNasa, Taylor Dearden, Fiona Dourif); outstanding guest actress in a drama series (Brittany Allen, Tal Anderson, Tina Ivlev) and more
Witherspoon says all you need is to watch one episode of “The Pitt,” HBO’s ER-set medical drama, to get the appeal. “You’ll be like, ‘Oh my God! I see how powerful this show is,’” he says.
The show’s second season follows senior attending doctor Dr. Michael “Robby” Robinavitch (Noah Wyle) on the last day before he heads out for a risky sabbatical.
Hidden Gems

Nominated for: Outstanding limited or anthology series; lead actress in an anthology series or movie (Sarah Snook); supporting actress in an anthology series or movie (Dakota Fanning); outstanding writing for a limited or anthology series (Meghan Gallagher)
The book “All Her Fault” was sparked by an incident from author Andrea Mara’s real life, which then became a Peacock miniseries. Sarah Snook plays a mom whose son disappears suddenly.
Witherspoon calls this a great show, and “one that you can rush through.”
Nominated for: Outstanding writing for a comedy series

The second season of “Jury Duty” followed the zany, “Truman Show”-esque premise of the first, but with a different setting. Instead of staging a fake jury duty, producers put the unsuspecting Anthony Norman at the center of a company retreat.
Must-See Performances

Maldonado and Witherspoon both said Noah Wyle is the one to watch in the outstanding lead actor in a drama category. He took away the award for “The Pitt’s” first season for his work as Dr. Michael “Robby” Robinavitch, the beleaguered, wise and occasionally bereft ER doctor.
Witherspoon also notes that he’s the first lead actor nominee who is also up for best director and could make history if he wins.

“Wonder Man” is a spin on a typical superhero show. Yahya Abdul-Mateen plays a struggling actor who ends up developing unexpected powers. The show was not renewed for a second season, a decision Abdul-Mateen has criticized. He was nominated for outstanding lead actor in a comedy series.

“It’s one of those shows that I think people underestimated. You know, it’s not getting a second season, but his performance is such a standout. He brings this like comedy and charm that I think is really refreshing,” Maldonado says.
Nominated for: Outstanding lead actor in a comedy series
Matthew Rhys is nominated for two Emmys this year: One for his work in the anthology series “The Beast in Me” and another for Apple TV’s sleeper hit “Widow’s Bay.”
“We’ve not really seen him be a nominee since ‘The Americans.’ I feel like it could put Matthew back in the winner circle,” Witherspoon says.
Nominated for: Outstanding supporting actress in a comedy series
“She just is so funny, so uncomfortable, so vulnerable, but also so badass. She’s been the MVP of the season of the show,” Maldonado says.
If you’re going to watch one episode, check out the episode “Beach Reads,” centered on her character discovering a bewitching book.
Nominated for: Outstanding lead actress in a drama series
Rhea Seehorn gives “such an impressive performance” as Carol Sturka, one of the few people not impacted by an alien virus, Maldonado says.
Witherspoon says she goes through “the entire range of emotions” on the show. Plus, her winning an Emmy would be a full-circle moment after years of nominations but no wins for “Better Call Saul.”

“I love when I watch moments where somebody who’s been in the game for 30 years gets their flowers. She’s 54 years old. She is the front runner to win that category. I just feel like give Rhea all her things,” Witherspoon says.

title: See Kelly Clarkson’s First TODAY Interview After Winning ‘American Idol’ 24 Years Ago
summary: Take a look back at Kelly Clarkson’s visit with TODAY, two days after she won the first season of “American Idol” in 2002.
story: Welcome to the “TODAY Archives,” where we revisit memories from our show when celebrities and newsmakers started discourse, made us laugh or shaped our culture. This latest installment aired Sept. 6, 2002 and features Kelly Clarkson, less than 48 hours after winning the first season of “American Idol.”

On Sept. 4, 2002, the world of music changed when Kelly Clarkson won the inaugural season of “American Idol.” Her charming, down-home personality and stunning vocal range won over viewers and judges alike, as Clarkson toppled Justin Guarini to win the show, which, like Clarkson herself, would go on to become a cultural institution.
